presentations.presentation_title: Changes in CO2 Balance with Natural Vegetation Succession After Severe Forest Disturbance
presentations.abstract: Forest ecosystems are expected to be a major sink of atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO 2 ), whereas their ability to absorb CO 2 is severely perturbed by artificial and natural disturbances, such as deforestation, fires, and windthrow. Many studies which adopted the chrono-sequence approach reported that such severe disturbances often changed forest to a large CO 2 source. However, there are few studies that directly measure CO 2 flux for a long term (more than a decade) above a disturbed forest site during secondary succession after severe disturbance.A flux site of a larch plantation in Hokkaido, northern Japan was struck by a typhoon in September 2004. Because of a severe windstorm, about 90% of trees fell. The fallen trees were removed by heavy machinery from the site, through which the soil surface and understory species were also disturbed. After the operations of timber transport, secondary succession progressed naturally in the ex-forest site. We recommenced flux measurement in August 2005. CO 2 flux has been measured by the eddy covariance technique with an open-path CO 2 / H 2 O analyzer (LI7500, Licor). Cumulative net ecosystem CO 2 exchange (NEE) during the growing season from May through October significantly decreased with time between 2006 and 2024. This decreasing trend was caused by the increase of gross primary production (GPP), which corresponded to vegetation recovery through secondary succession; dominant plant species changed from small shrubs to deciduous broadleaf trees.

presentations.presentation_title: Multi-scale Climatic Trends Preceding Glacial Lake Outburst Floods Across High Mountain Asia: Insights from Four Case Studies
presentations.institution: Seto Inland Sea Carbon Neutral Research Center (S-CNC), Graduate School of Innovation and Practice for Smart Society (SmaSo), Hiroshima University, Higashi-Hiroshima, Hiroshima 739-8529 Japan
presentations.abstract: Glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) are sudden, high-magnitude releases of water from glacial lakes triggered by external forcings such as avalanches, intense rainfall, or rapid ice melting, and they pose an escalating hazard in high‐mountain regions under climate change. High Mountain Asia (HMA), the “Third Pole”, covers 4.2 million km², contains more than 30,000 glacial lakes, and sustains ten major river basins. Rapid glacier mass loss and glacier expansion underscore the need to clarify the climatic conditions that preceded GLOFs.This study investigates multi‐scale climatic trends associated with both ice- and moraine-dammed lake failures across the HMA. Four representative case studies were analyzed: Mezbacher Lake (annually draining), Shisper Lake (recurrent events since 2019), Chorabari Lake (June 2013), and South Lhonak Lake (October 2023). Using ERA5 reanalysis, CRU-TS, MODIS and related datasets, we assessed long-term trends (1961–2023) in near-surface air and land surface temperatures, precipitation, snowfall and surface energy budgets, together with 30-day anomalies prior to each GLOF event.All sites exhibited a strong regional and local warming signal (~0.03 °C yr⁻¹). No consistent long-term precipitation trend was detected, although snowfall locally declined at several sites. Moraine-dammed lakes failures are consistently preceded by elevated temperatures and pronounced short-term temperature anomalies. Chorabari Lake also shows an extreme precipitation spike immediately prior to collapse. In contrast, ice-dammed lakes showed weaker or absent short-term anomaly, despite clear long-term warming.These findings suggest that rising temperatures, reduced snowfall, and episodic precipitation are key climatic precursors for moraine-dammed GLOFs, whereas ice-dammed systems appear less sensitive to short-term meteorological triggers. Ongoing work integrates detailed surface energy balance analyses and satellite-derived snow and water indices to better resolve failure mechanisms and improve GLOF hazard predictions under continued warming.

presentations.presentation_title: Making Dynamic Vegetation Models More Accessible: the SEIB-explorer Run-and-view Environment
presentations.abstract: Dynamic Global Vegetation Models (DGVMs) play a central role in assessing ecosystem responses to climate change, yet their increasing complexity and technical requirements often limit their accessibility beyond specialist communities. In this presentation, I introduce SEIB-Explorer, a standalone platform that couples the execution of the individual-based SEIB-DGVM with interactive three-dimensional visualization and lightweight analysis tools. The software provides a graphical user interface that streamlines model execution and result exploration, lowering the barrier to entry for non-specialists. SEIB-Explorer enables users to visualize forest structure at a single site as a virtual stand, with plant functional types clearly distinguished and temporal changes examined through an interactive time slider. Multiple information panels summarize model metadata, annual fluxes, and time series of carbon, water, and vegetation-related variables. A visually enhanced display mode further supports interpretability for educational use and public engagement. By integrating model execution, visualization, and basic exploratory analysis within a single environment, SEIB-Explorer reduces technical and cognitive overhead while promoting reproducible workflows and interdisciplinary exchange. This approach demonstrates how improved accessibility and interpretability can broaden the impact of DGVMs in research, education, and outreach contexts.

presentations.presentation_title: Atmospheric CO₂ Growth Response to the Three-year Consecutive La Niña Events During 2020–2022
presentations.institution: Graduate School of Environmental Studies, Nagoya University
presentations.abstract: The atmospheric CO₂ growth rate represents the net balance between anthropogenic emissions and natural carbon uptake by land and ocean. Its interannual variability is strongly modulated by climate modes, such as the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO). During the strong La Niña event in 2011, the CO₂ growth rate anomaly reached -0.914 PgC/year, largely attributed to enhanced terrestrial carbon uptake in semi-arid regions. From 2020 to 2022, a rare triple-dip La Niña event occurred, with ENSO indices comparable in magnitude to 2011. Contrary to expectations, however, the CO₂ growth rate anomaly during this period was only -0.555 PgC/year, substantially weaker than the 2011 response. This discrepancy has not been systematically examined. Here, we investigate the dominant contributors and underlying mechanisms using a bottom-up reconstruction approach. We statistically combine major carbon-cycle components, fossil fuel emissions, land-use change emissions, fire emissions, land net ecosystem exchange (NEE), and ocean-atmosphere CO₂ fluxes- based on the Global Carbon Budget 2024 dataset. Only a limited subset of components reproduces the observed variability in the NOAA based CO₂ growth rate. Analysis of the reconstructed growth rates reveals that La Niña-induced enhancement of land carbon uptake was markedly weaker during 2020-2022 than in 2011, differing by 1.2 PgC/year. Yet, this reduced alone cannot fully explain the muted atmospheric response. We further identify a simultaneous weakening of ocean carbon uptake, particularly a pronounced decline in the Southern Ocean sink. The concurrent reductions in both terrestrial and oceanic carbon uptake point to a shift in the ENSO-carbon cycle relationship, indicating that natural sinks have recently become less effective at offsetting atmospheric CO₂ increases during La Niña conditions. This emerging change has important implications for the future variability and resilience of the global carbon cycle.

presentations.presentation_title: What 20 Years of Flux Measurements Reveal about Carbon–Water Coupling in Permafrost Forests
presentations.abstract: Rapid warming at northern high latitudes is accompanied by changes in the hydrological cycle and rising atmospheric CO₂ concentrations, with profound implications for carbon and water exchanges in permafrost ecosystems. Decadal observations are essential for identifying ecosystem trajectories under such compound environmental forcing. In this talk, we present insights from more than two decades of quasi-continuous eddy covariance measurements beginning in 2003, conducted over a poorly drained black spruce forest on permafrost peat in interior Alaska, with a focus on multi-decadal changes in CO₂ exchange and evapotranspiration (ET). Over the initial two decades of observation, the forest acted as a small net CO₂ sink (−53 ± 63 g C m⁻² yr⁻¹), with a clear increase in CO₂ uptake from the first to the second decade (Ueyama et al., 2024; PNAS). This increase was primarily driven by an enhancement in gross primary productivity (GPP), associated with anomalously wet conditions resulting from recent increases in precipitation and potentially reflecting hydrologically driven vegetation changes in this poorly drained system. In addition, rising atmospheric CO₂ contributed a detectable fertilization effect, explaining approximately 3% of the observed GPP increase. Alongside the increased CO₂ sink, ET has also increased over the same period, indicating an intensifying coupling between carbon and water cycles. However, the long-term trend in ET has not kept pace with the rate of increasing precipitation, indicating a growing imbalance in the surface water budget and potential shifts in energy partitioning and soil moisture regimes. These findings highlight how gradual wetting and rising CO₂ jointly reshape ecosystem function in permafrost forests and demonstrate the unique value of long-term flux observations for constraining future projections of high-latitude carbon–water feedbacks.

presentations.presentation_title: Seasonal Dynamics of Forest Plant Traits from Spaceborne Hyperspectral Observations
presentations.abstract: Plant functional traits are key indicators of vegetation responses to environmental variability. Airborne hyperspectral data enable accurate trait mapping but are limited in spatial and temporal coverage. Spaceborne hyperspectral observations provide new opportunities for large-scale, seasonal monitoring. We developed a multi-stage framework integrating PRISMA spaceborne hyperspectral imagery with NEON Airborne Observation Platform data to quantify seasonal dynamics of four forest plant traits, including chlorophyll, carotenoids, equivalent water thickness, and nitrogen, across eleven NEON sites spanning diverse forest types and ecoregions in the contiguous United States. Spaceborne-derived trait estimates showed strong agreement with airborne benchmarks (R² = 0.78–0.88; NRMSE = 5.4–8.4%). Results revealed consistent seasonal patterns across traits and forest types, with variability driven primarily by climate factors and soil properties. These findings demonstrate the potential of spaceborne hyperspectral data for scalable, seasonal monitoring of forest plant functional traits.

presentations.presentation_title: Geospatial Data-integrated Observation System for Pine Wilt Disease Detection using Traffic CCTV Networks and Deep Learning
presentations.abstract: As forests play an increasingly important role as carbon sinks, tree mortality from Pine Wilt Disease (PWD) has become a critical concern in Korea. PWD-induced forest losses create substantial uncertainties in national greenhouse gas inventory and mitigation planning. While early detection and rapid response are essential to prevent the spread of PWD, traditional monitoring methods mostly field surveys, face significant temporal and economic constraints for continuous large-scale observation. Most recently, drone- and satellite-based remote sensing has expanded spatial coverage, but these approaches remain limited in their ability to resolve fine-scale temporal dynamics of PWD. To overcome these limitations, this study proposes a near-real-time monitoring system that repurposes existing traffic CCTV infrastructure as near-surface remote sensing sensors. The methodology employs deep learning-based image segmentation models identify dead-tree signatures within CCTV footage, followed by multi-temporal validation logic to filter out noise from individual frames and detect new PWD outbreaks. Furthermore, the system performs geocoding based on the installation coordinates of CCTV cameras and spatially cross-referenced these results with national pest management history data to identify new outbreaks currently excluded from official management records. This system offers a strategic advantage by maximizing existing infrastructure without additional equipment, thereby effectively eliminating observation blind spots. Thereby enabling earlier intervention and targeted disease management. It is expected to serve as a crucial decision-support tool for protecting carbon sinks through early identification of PWD front lines and for refining the precision of national carbon statistics.

presentations.presentation_title: Decadal Spectral Reflectance and NDVI Dynamics in an Interior Alaska Black Spruce Forest: Ground Observations and Gcom-c/sgli Validation
presentations.institution: Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Air temperature in the high latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere has increased at a rate higher than the global mean, and recent studies indicate warming of approximately three to four times the global average. In this context, it is important to understand how subarctic coniferous forests in the Arctic–boreal region respond to ongoing climate change. Earth observation satellites provide an essential tool for large-scale monitoring of ecosystem dynamics, but remote high-latitude regions have limited field sites for validation, highlighting the importance of long-term ground-based observations. In this study, we analyzed changes in vegetation spectral reflectance over the past decade using long-term in situ spectroradiometric measurements collected from 2015 to 2025 (11 years) in an evergreen coniferous black spruce forest in interior Alaska. We compared the in situ reflectance and NDVI with satellite-based products derived from the JAXA Second-generation Global Imager (SGLI). No clear long-term trends were detected in the timing of spring snowmelt or the onset of green-up at the study site. Snowmelt timing was strongly influenced by interannual variability in snow accumulation, particularly during the latter half of winter, and increased snow accumulation since 2016 may have offset potential advances in spring phenology. Seasonal variations in reflectance and NDVI derived from ground observations were in good agreement with those from SGLI, indicating that satellite products adequately represent current phenological seasonality in and around the site. NDVI rapidly increased after snowmelt, gradually rose to a late-July peak, and then decreased toward autumn. Notably, NDVI remained stable during late August to September despite visible understory color changes, forming a plateau period consistent with a phenomenon suggested by our previous theoretical work.

presentations.presentation_title: Biophysical Variations in Land Surface and Soil Temperature Induced by Vegetation Greening on the Qinghai-tibet Plateau Over 2003-2023
presentations.abstract: The Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau (QTP), known as the "Third Pole", has experienced significant greening over recent decades. Vegetation changes alter soil thermal regimes through modification of surface energy balance, with potentially large climate feedbacks. However, the seasonal relationships between surface and subsurface temperature responses to vegetation greening remain poorly understood in the region. This study quantifies the sensitivity of Land Surface Temperature (LST) and Soil Temperatures (ST) at multiple depths (0-7, 7-28, and 28-100 cm) to Leaf Area Index (LAI) variations across grassland ecosystems on the QTP by integrating long-term observational data (2003-2023) with a space-for-time moving window approach. We applied machine learning algorithms to reduce systematic biases in ERA5-Land ST. Results reveal a pronounced seasonal asymmetry in temperature sensitivity: vegetation greening in the alpine grasslands induces a warming effect during the Dormant Season (DS) and a cooling effect during the Growing Season (GS) for both LST and ST. Furthermore, a pronounced nonlinear relationship exists between LAI and GS sensitivity across all layers. Sparsely vegetated areas (steppes) exhibit the strongest cooling sensitivity, while densely vegetated areas (meadows) show reduced cooling sensitivity approaching zero during GS. Grassland greening induces greater warming in ST than in LST, with the strongest sensitivity in the near-surface layer (0-7 cm) than in the deeper soils. ST sensitivity to greening increases with depth from 0.18±0.23 to 0.20±0.28 °C.m².m - ² during the GS and decreases significantly with depth from 1.51±0.38 to 1.07±0.15 °C.m².m - ² during the DS. The annual transition between warming and cooling regimes is governed by hydroclimatic conditions, suggesting that the boundary between these regimes may shift under future climate change. These findings highlight the complex biophysical feedbacks of vegetation change on the thermal environment and have important implications for regional climate modeling and ecosystem management in the QTP.

presentations.presentation_title: Phenology-driven Source-free Unsupervised Domain Adaptation Framework for Cross-regional Rice Mapping
presentations.institution: Department of Civil Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology of Madras
presentations.abstract: Accurate crop type mapping at regional scales is critical for food security monitoring, yet it is often constrained by limited labeled training data and pronounced spectral–temporal variability arising from domain shifts across regions. While unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) methods facilitate knowledge transfer from label-rich source regions to label-scarce target regions, existing source-free UDA (SFUDA) frameworks primarily rely on statistical feature alignment and largely overlook the key biological driver of domain shift namely, displacement of crop phenology due to climatic and management variability. This study proposes a phenology-aware source-free domain adaptation framework for rice mapping that explicitly incorporates crop growth dynamics to enable robust cross-regional transfer without accessing source-domain data during adaptation. A pre-trained deep learning model is employed as a fixed backbone. For an unlabeled target domain, fused Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2–derived temporal signatures are analyzed to identify key phenological transition points, which are used to decompose pixel-level time series into individual rice growth cycles. From each cycle, stage-normalized phenological descriptors are extracted, enabling crop identification based on growth behavior rather than absolute calendar timing. These phenology-normalized representations are subsequently adapted using a mutual information–based objective that balances prediction confidence and class diversity, resulting in stable and discriminative inference in the target domain. Unlike conventional SFUDA approaches that operate directly on raw, calendar-aligned time-series features, the proposed framework introduces phenology-driven biological normalization as an intermediate adaptation mechanism, effectively decoupling rice identification from sowing and harvesting dates. The framework is evaluated across heterogeneous rice-growing regions characterized by asynchronous cropping calendars and varying establishment practices. Results demonstrate that incorporating explicit phenological normalization substantially reduces negative transfer caused by seasonal temporal shifts and improves cross-regional rice classification performance relative to baseline SFUDA methods. Integrating phenology-driven SFUDA enables scalable and biologically interpretable rice mapping in diverse, data-sparse regions.

presentations.presentation_title: A Global 500 m Dataset of Tree Crown Morphology for Earth System Modeling
presentations.abstract: Tree crown architecture varies widely across the globe and plays a vital role in land-atmosphere interactions, particularly during snow-covered periods. Canopy structure strongly controls the interception, masking and shading of snow, making it challenging to simulate snow-season forest surface albedo in Earth system models. However, commonly used structural proxies (e.g. leaf area index and canopy cover) have been shown to be insufficient to constrain snow-albedo feedback.Here, we develop a globally consistent 500 m crown structure dataset of crown depth (CD), crown width (CW) and aspect ratio (AR=CD/CW), and demonstrate its value for improving snow–vegetation radiative processes in the Common Land Model (CoLM2024). Using Random Forest-based allometric models driven by satellite-derived canopy height and bioclimatic variables, we upscale over 340,000 field observations of CD and CW into global maps. The RF models outperform traditional allometric equations, increasing R² by 0.58 and reducing RMSE by 18% for boreal trees. AR remains relatively stable across canopy height classes while showing strong climatic sensitivity, highlighting its potential as a robust descriptor of 3D crown shape for large-scale modeling. The resulting AR map also reveals deep, narrow crowns in boreal forests (mean AR = 1.8±0.7) and wide, shallow crowns in temperate regions (mean AR = 0.95±0.4). Evaluation against an ESM-SnowMIP forest site shows that incorporating AR into CoLM2024 to represent canopy structure enhances canopy radiative absorption and substantially reduces the overestimation of snow-season albedo, decreasing bias by 57% and RMSE by 32%.Overall, this dataset provides a practical structural constraint for Earth system models to better represent snow–vegetation radiative coupling and a valuable benchmark for forest structural diversity studies.

presentations.presentation_title: Remotely Sensed Environmental and Ecological Issues Over the Past Two Decades in the Lower Mekong River Basin
presentations.abstract: Among the most biodiverse environments in the world, the Mekong River Basin has experienced extensive socio-economic development in the past few decades resulting in land use change and associated ecological and environmental stresses. To assess possible impacts on sensitive ecosystems and their services in the Lower Mekong River Basin (LMB), we examine spatial and temporal changes in forest community extent, as well as tree density and canopy coverage, in relation to carbon uptake and climate change. We employed the Mann–Kendall test to identify regions of likely significant ecological and environmental change within forest ecosystems. We developed a new approach to eliminate the classification of false positives and false negatives. We quantified the annual rate of ecological changes using Sen’s slope. Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression analysis was performed to analyze the impact of tree and leaf density changes on the regional environment, particularly with regard to net primary productivity (NPP) and surface temperature trends. Across the LMB, a total of 2.81% of forest extent has been lost. Cambodia experienced the most prominent forest loss among all countries, while Thailand and Myanmar had net forest gain. NPP trends were starkly divergent from the north to the south and declined across the majority of northern Laos. The LMB region experienced increasing trends for both daytime and nighttime temperatures except for small portions of Thailand and Vietnam. An annual 0.0876°C increase in surface temperature can be expected for every 1% decrease in tree density in forest degraded regions, while a substantial annual carbon productivity increase can be expected in reforested regions. In addition, the effectiveness of policy enforcement at the government level is critical for reforestation in LMB.

presentations.presentation_title: Stress Trajectory Typology of Mangrove Canopy Condition Across Indonesia from Sentinel Time Series
presentations.abstract: Indonesia’s mangroves provide coastal protection, livelihoods, and contribute to blue carbon storage. However, mangrove conditions are increasingly shaped by interactions among inland and marine pressures and anthropogenic land-use change. National monitoring often emphasizes extent, leaving a limited understanding of how mangrove canopy condition evolves through time and where stress is persistent versus transient. This study develops a Sentinel-based framework to derive a national typology of mangrove canopy condition stress trajectories across Indonesia. Using the Global Mangrove Watch 2020 extent as a fixed analysis domain, the workflow is implemented in Google Earth Engine. A high-frequency composite time series is constructed using 14-day windows from 2017 to the most recent available observations, with cloud and shadow impacts minimized through compositing and quality screening. Mangrove Canopy condition is quantified using a composite score derived from seven Sentinel-2 indices capturing complementary dimensions of vegetation vigor, chlorophyll-sensitive response, moisture-related stress, and background robustness. Seasonal baselines are estimated to separate expected wet–dry behavior from abnormal departures, producing standardized anomaly time series. Trajectory typologies are derived by extracting time-series features describing seasonal amplitude, anomaly intensity, persistence and recurrence, recovery behavior, and long-term trend, and classifying pixels into a small set of interpretable regimes. Sentinel-1 SAR is integrated at a supporting level to provide cloud-robust context related to moisture/inundation conditions and potential structural change. Expected outputs include a national map of stress trajectory types, regional summaries across island groups, and identification of persistent stress hotspots. These products provide an empirical basis for subsequent inland–coastal coupling analyses by enabling screening of relationships between mangrove stress regimes and hydroclimatic or watershed-linked drivers.

presentations.presentation_title: SDCI: Improved Monitoring of Crop Leaf Chlorophyll Content via a Novel Vegetation Index
presentations.abstract: Accurate estimation of crop leaf chlorophyll content (LCC) is crucial for monitoring crop growth status and agricultural management. Dynamic, non-destructive, and efficient monitoring of LCC using remote sensing vegetation indices (VIs) has become a vital component of agricultural information management. In canopy-level remote sensing observations, the apparent reflectance received by sensors results from the deep coupling between leaf biochemical components and canopy structural properties. Currently, empirical models based on vegetation indices (VIs) offer the most widely used method for efficiently correlating spectral features with LCC. However, the spectral response characteristics of the canopy are simultaneously influenced by the coupling effects of LCC and the canopy structure (e.g., leaf area index (LAI)), making the VI-LCC relationship unstable under varying observation conditions. This study proposes a novel Structural-Decoupled Chlorophyll Index (SDCI) through a “first-order decoupling and secondary correction” approach, aiming to address the issues of “spectral signal contamination” and “nonlinear saturation” in LCC estimation caused by LAI variations. Specifically, a red-edge-based vegetation index (VIRE) serves as the biochemical signal source, designed to capture subtle changes in pigment-level absorption. Given the susceptibility of red-edge signals to soil background and stray light radiation, this study introduces the Optimized Soil-Adjusted Vegetation Index (OSAVI) as a structural baseline operator. To mitigate path length deviations caused by multiple scattering in non-Lambertian media, a new vegetation index based on weighted geometric mean is proposed within the context of first-order decoupling. Analyses combining radiative transfer model simulations and multi-site field data from China demonstrate that the first-order decoupling effectively eliminates linear geometric interference and remains unaffected by LAI changes. The secondary correction maintains sensitivity to LCC while significantly reducing sensitivity to LAI. Consequently, the constructed SDCI index achieves enhanced accuracy in LCC retrieval compared to traditional VIs, providing a new and reliable tool for monitoring the crop growth status.

presentations.presentation_title: Ecosystem-scale Carbon Balance to Improve Emission Factors for Acacia Plantations on Tropical Peatlands
presentations.abstract: Peatlands are among the most carbon-rich terrestrial ecosystems, yet managed peatlands used for agriculture and silviculture are significant sources of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Southeast Asia contains approximately one-third of the world’s tropical peatlands, with nearly half managed to support economic development and population growth. Despite their importance, large uncertainties persist in emission estimates, potentially driven by limited field measurements – and also the predominant reliance on indirect peat carbon loss estimates derived from short-term soil flux chamber and subsidence approaches. As a result, current IPCC Tier 1 emission factors (EFs) for tropical peatlands may not adequately represent ecosystem-scale carbon dynamics, underscoring the need to strengthen Tier 3 Measurement, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) systems.Since 2016, we have implemented an integrated, long-term GHG observation program in an Acacia crassicarpa plantation on tropical peatland in Sumatra, Indonesia. Net ecosystem exchanges of CO 2 and CH 4 were quantified using eddy covariance systems with continuous 30-minute measurements, complemented by chamber-based measurements of soil N 2 O. These observations enabled quantification of the comprehensive ecosystem-scale GHG balance over a complete plantation rotation.When carbon export via harvested wood was accounted for as emissions, the plantation exhibited GHG emissions more than 60% lower than IPCC Tier 1 EFs. Partial utilization of harvested biomass for bioenergy could further reduce the overall climate impact. These findings indicate that current IPCC emission factors may overestimate emissions from existing Acacia plantations on tropical peatlands. Incorporating ecosystem-scale observations and full plantation-rotation assessments into Tier 3 EF development substantially improves the accuracy and credibility of GHG accounting for managed tropical peatland ecosystems.

presentations.presentation_title: Global Natural Wetland Methane Fluxes (2000-2025): Insights for Asia
presentations.abstract: Wetland methane (CH4) emissions are highly variable and critical to the global CH4 budget, yet low-latency estimates remain scarce, especially for regions such as Asia and Southeast Asia where wetlands and peatlands are extensive and climate variability is strong. We present a low-latency global freshwater wetland CH4 flux dataset at monthly, 1°×1° resolution for 2000–2025, and highlight its application for regional assessment across Asia. This dataset enables: (1) analysis of spatial–temporal variations in wetland CH4 emissions globally and across Asia, including identification of regional hotspots; (2) quantification of flux responses to climate variability and extremes; and (3) exploration of large-scale teleconnections, especially ENSO-related hydroclimate variability, and their impacts on wetland CH4. Overall, our approach provides timely flux estimates to advance process understanding, model evaluation, and climate–carbon feedback assessments, while supporting regionally focused analyses relevant to the Asia–Oceania domain.

presentations.presentation_title: Analysing the Unique Pattern of Fossil Fuel Emissions in Pakistan and Causes Behind It
presentations.institution: Graduate School of Innovation and Practice for Smart Society (SmaSo), Hiroshima University, Higashi-Hiroshima, Hiroshima 739-8529 Japan
presentations.abstract: Pakistan’s recent fossil-fuel CO₂ emissions exhibit a distinct, non-monotonic trajectory compared to regional and global patterns. Using EDGAR v8 emissions data together with national energy and industrial indicators, this study identified four structural phases in Pakistan’s emissions pathway: stabilization (2007–2014), a sharp decline in 2019, a rebound (2019–2022), and a renewed decline from 2023 onward. These shifts represent structural breaks rather than normal interannual variability.From 2000 onward, emissions rose steadily, driven by rapid urbanization, industrialization, and the growing demand for electricity and transport fuels. The 2007-2014 plateau occurred despite continued population growth and reflected prolonged energy shortages, macroeconomic stagnation, worsening security conditions, reduced investor confidence, and declining foreign direct investment in manufacturing and construction. After 2014, emissions resumed growth alongside economic recovery, infrastructure expansion under the China Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), increased coal- and RLNG-based power generation, and rising transport and industrial activity.A critical turning point emerged in 2018–2019, when power generation shifted away from furnace oil toward RLNG, hydropower, nuclear energy, renewables, and new coal capacity, sharply reducing fuel-oil use and emissions in the power sector. Simultaneously, macroeconomic stabilization measures, including currency depreciation, high interest rates, and import compression suppressed energy-intensive manufacturing and construction, amplifying the 2019 decline. The renewed decrease from 2023 is linked to steep electricity tariff hikes, IMF-driven fiscal tightening, greater reliance on domestic energy resources and reduced freight and transport activityOverall, Pakistan’s emissions trajectory is governed less by smooth long-term growth and more by sectorial energy transitions interacting with economic shocks, governance constraints, and policy reforms. Understanding these dynamics is essential for designing robust strategies that reconcile climate mitigation with economic stability and energy security issues.Keywords: Fossil fuel emissions; Emission trends; Energy consumption; Macroeconomic stabilization; Energy policy; Industrial growth; Environmental sustainability.

presentations.presentation_title: Thailand’s Greenhouse Gas Budget in Transition: From Land-Use–Dominated to Fossil-Energy–Dominated Emissions
presentations.abstract: National greenhouse-gas (GHG) assessments need consistent accounting of CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O across fossil energy, land-use change, and ecosystem processes. For Thailand, relevant evidence is dispersed across inventories and research products that differ in system boundaries and land-flux treatment. Here we synthesize the literature and compile an integrated, multi-gas GHG budget for Thailand by harmonizing CO₂, CH₄ and N₂O sources, summarized for the 2000s and 2010s in the context of long-term trends. The synthesis indicates that Thailand’s GHG balance increased from the 2000s to the 2010s and shifted toward fossil-energy dominance, with growth concentrated in power generation and road transport and sustained contributions across major fuels. CH₄ is dominated by agriculture and waste, while N₂O is dominated by agricultural soils. In the land sector, bookkeeping estimates suggest declining ELUC since the early 2000s, while vegetation-flux estimates indicate that changes in biospheric uptake can offset part of land-use emission reductions. Overall, the integrated budget highlights the need to address fossil energy alongside managed-land CH₄ and N₂O, while tracking land-sector carbon dynamics when evaluating Thailand’s mitigation pathway and national targets.

presentations.presentation_title: Greenhouse Gas Budget Assessment of Myanmar for 2000-2019
presentations.abstract: Reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions is an urgent challenge for climate change mitigation. However, national-scale GHG budgets remain poorly quantified in many developing countries. Myanmar is characterized by extensive forest areas, rapid deforestation, and economic and structural change, leading to large uncertainties in the balance between GHG sources and sinks. To date, no comprehensive multi-gas GHG budget assessment has been conducted for Myanmar. This study provides the first national GHG budget assessment for Myanmar for the period 2000–2019, integrating carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), and nitrous oxide (N₂O). This study examined whether Myanmar acts as a net GHG source or sink, identified the dominant sources and sinks, and evaluated the implications of Myanmar’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) toward carbon neutrality under the Paris Agreement. The analysis followed the RECCAP2 framework for Southeast Asia (Kondo et al., 2025) and integrated multiple global datasets covering anthropogenic and biospheric fluxes. Myanmar was identified as a net GHG source during 2000–2019, with total emissions of 445 ± 213 Tg CO₂-equivalent yr⁻¹. Fire emissions were the dominant source, followed by deforestation and wood harvest; together, these accounted for approximately 70% of total gross emissions. Despite significant CO₂ uptake through vegetation and forest regrowth, these sinks were insufficient to offset gross emissions. Fossil fuel emissions contributed only a small proportion of total gross emissions. Comparison with Myanmar’s NDC indicates that current mitigation strategies mainly focus on the energy and forest and land-use sectors, while fire emissions and non-CO₂ gases (CH₄ and N₂O) are not fully considered. These results suggest that Myanmar’s pathway toward carbon neutrality depends more strongly on the management of fires and land-use change.

presentations.presentation_title: Declining Co₂ Outgassing in the Northwestern Indian Ocean-the Oman-somalia Upwelling Zone
presentations.institution: Graduate School of Innovation and Practice for Smart Society (SmaSo). hiroshima University
presentations.abstract: The Oman–Somalia upwelling system in the northwestern Indian Ocean (NIO: 0–30°N, 38–78°E) is a major hotspot for CO₂ outgassing during the summer southwest monsoon season. Empirical air–sea CO₂ fluxes from the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA), driven by JRA-55 reanalysis wind product, showed a declining trend in summer outgassing from 1990 to 2023, accompanied by an increase in winter.To evaluate the robustness of these seasonal trends, we compared the JMA results with the SeaFlux harmonized dataset (1990–2019), which provides 30 flux estimates derived from combinations of five wind products and six surface ocean pCO₂ (spCO₂) datasets, including JMA/JRA-55. Unlike the original JMA product, SeaFlux does not reveal strong seasonally contrasting long-term trends in the data. Most SeaFlux members indicated declining summer fluxes, but a systematic winter increase appeared only in a limited subset of JMA-based combinations.Grouping SeaFlux results by spCO₂ product showed that wind product choice primarily altered flux magnitude while leaving interannual variability and trend direction largely intact. In contrast, different spCO₂ datasets produce substantial discrepancies in both variability and long-term trends, highlighting spCO₂ as the dominant source of uncertainty in the data. A comparison between the original JMA fluxes and SeaFlux-derived JMA combinations confirmed consistent year-to-year variability but notably weaker summer trends in the harmonized framework.These findings underscore significant uncertainties in regional air–sea CO₂ flux estimation for the upwelling system, largely driven by differences among spCO₂ products rather than winds. They motivate further investigation of original spCO₂ datasets, focusing specifically on the core upwelling zone (~4–21°N, 52–66°E) instead of the broader northwestern Indian Ocean, to better isolate seasonally driven CO₂ responses and improve confidence in regional carbon flux assessments.

presentations.presentation_title: Progress in National GHG Budget Assessment of Southeast Asia and Its Applications to Policy Making on Rice Production
presentations.abstract: Southeast Asia is one of the world’s most important rice-producing regions, underpinning regional food security, rural livelihoods, and cultural traditions. At the same time, rice paddies are recognized as a major anthropogenic source of methane (CH₄). Consequently, CH₄ emissions from rice cultivation occupy a prominent position in national greenhouse gas (GHG) inventories and have become a focal point of climate policy under the UNFCCC. However, imposing strict mitigation obligations on rice production may adversely affect food production and social stability, underscoring the need to balance climate mitigation with food security. This study addresses a fundamental question: Is it appropriate to regulate rice cultivation–derived CH₄ emissions in Southeast Asia as strictly as emissions from other sectors? Recognizing that maintaining current rice production inevitably entails a certain level of CH₄ emissions, we aim to provide an integrated scientific assessment to inform realistic and socially acceptable climate policy design. The research is structured around two main pillars. First, we conduct a comprehensive assessment of major GHG emission processes in Southeast Asian countries—including rice cultivation, fossil fuel combustion, waste management, deforestation, and anthropogenic fires—by integrating national statistics, satellite observations, and model simulations compiled under the League of geophysical research eXcellences for tropical asia (LeXtra). Second, we develop cross-sectoral mitigation scenarios to evaluate whether climate neutrality can be achieved through enhanced reductions in non-agricultural sectors, even if rice-related CH₄ emissions are not substantially reduced. By integrating natural and social sciences, this study moves beyond sector-specific and qualitative discussions. It provides quantitative evidence on trade-offs between climate mitigation and food security, proposes alternative policy pathways that avoid excessive burdens on rice farmers, and offers strategic insights applicable not only to Southeast Asia but also to other agriculture-dependent regions.

presentations.presentation_title: Towards Robust Understanding of Co2 Budget
presentations.abstract: Robust quantification of the land and ocean CO 2 sink is critical for projecting future climate change and informing effective mitigation strategies. A major challenge lies in reliably partitioning the global land and ocean CO 2 fluxes. Estimates derived from atmospheric inversion and process-based models often diverge, ranging from week to strong sink estimates. Moreover, fossil-fuel CO₂ (FCO₂) emissions—typically prescribed as nearly certain in CO 2 -budget analyses—remain uncertain in both magnitude and trends, propagating biases in inferred land and ocean fluxes. To investigate these biases and the sensitivity of land-ocean partioning to choice of prior fluxes, we conducted a series of CO 2 inversion using combinations of: two land-biospheric priors (cyclostationary CASA and interannully varying MiCASA), two ocean priors (one cyclostationary from upscaled pCO2 observations, and one interannually varying from an empirical model of JMA), and three interannually varying FCO 2 fields (GridFED, EDGAR, and ODIAC). Choice of ocean priors had a significant influence on estimated land biospheric fluxes, as the ocean a posteriori fluxes remained close to the chosen prior. Specifically, stronger ocean priors led to weaker inferred land sinks, and vice versa — highlighting their coupled sensitivity in an inversion system that is under-determined due to lack of high quality measurements covering the globe. In contrast, ocean flux estimates remained largely insensitive to the choice of land prior. Additionally, bias in FCO₂ emissions strongly affect both the magnitude and trends of inferred land fluxes.

presentations.presentation_title: Ghg Budget Assessment of Vietnam
presentations.abstract: To combat climate change, nations worldwide have committed to mitigating and regulating greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions under the Paris Agreement, aiming to achieve carbon neutrality. However, transitioning from conceptual commitments to practical implementation remains uncertain for developing nations, largely because of limitations in technology and human resources. Vietnam, a rapidly developing economy in Southeast Asia, has experienced remarkable economic growth with GDP increasing from $93 billion to $315 billion between 2000 and 2019, sustaining an average annual growth rate of approximately 5–7%. Under these circumstances, intergrating environmental protection strategies and robust GHG accounting into national economic planning has become increasingly critical to ensure sustainable development.Our study is the first to estimates a comprehensive GHG budget for carbon dioxide (CO 2 ), methane (CH 4 ), and nitrous oxide (N 2 O) for Vietnam over the period of 2000 to 2019 using aggregated multi-source datasets. CO 2 emissions accounted for 70% of total gross GHG emissions, with deforestation the dominant source, followed by anthropogenic fire emissions. Emissions from fossil fuel use, primarily coal, increased substantially, more than doubling from the 2000s to the 2010s, thereby turning the biosphere into a net CO 2 source. Meanwhile, CH 4 and N 2 O exhibited persistent net emissions throughout the study period. CH 4 emissions from rice cultivation showed a modest decling trend, while N 2 O emissions remained the smallest contributor to the overall GHG budget.Overall, Vietnam’s total GHG budget over the past 20 years amounted to a net source of 406.8 68.2 TgCO 2 eq yr -1 . This highlights the pressure Vietnam faces in reconciling rapid economic growth with effective GHG mitigation. By accounting for both anthropogenic and natural emissions, our study provides policymakers with a comprehensive overview of Vietnam's emission profile and supports urgent mitigation actions, particularly in land-use changes and coal consumption, to secure a viable pathway toward climate neutrality.

presentations.presentation_title: Photochemical Fate of Land-to-ocean Dissolved Organic Matter: Formation of Recalcitrant Carboxyl-rich Alicyclic Molecules
presentations.abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) plays a critical role in the global carbon cycle. Rivers deliver substantial fluxes of terrestrial DOM to the ocean, where it is processed through both photochemical and microbial transformations into refractory DOM (r-DOM), a long-lived material that sequesters carbon in the deep ocean for millennia. While these processes are fundamental to long-term carbon storage, the molecular-level formation mechanisms of r-DOM remain poorly understood, particularly for carboxyl-rich alicyclic molecules (CRAM), a major constituent of the marine r-DOM pool. This study provides a comprehensive mechanistic analysis of the photochemical pathway to CRAM formation. Using Fourier-transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR-MS) and ¹⁸O-isotope labeling, we tracked the photochemical modification of terrestrial, microbial, and coastal DOM samples. Photoproducts incorporating 18 O exhibited lower molecular weight, lower double bond equivalence (DBE), and higher O/C ratios, aligning with photodegradation pathways that produce aliphatic acids such as CRAM. Tandem MS analysis of 369 precursor ions (m/z 200–500) further revealed prevalent neutral losses of CO 2 and H 2 O, particularly among lower molecular weight species. A key finding emerged from isotopomer analysis: a majority of carboxyl (55%) and hydroxyl (67%) oxygen atoms retained native 16 O after irradiation, with only ~45% of carboxyl groups incorporating 18 O. This indicates that the acidic functionalities in photochemically produced CRAM are not solely derived from external oxygen. Instead, photochemical reactions selectively preserve and concentrate pre-existing, structurally stable acidic moieties. We conclude that photochemically-driven CRAM formation proceeds primarily through the structural reorganization of native DOM, rather than complete or partial oxidation. This selective photochemical oxidation stabilizes specific functional groups, contributing to molecular recalcitrance. These findings provide novel and critical constraints on one of the key abiotic formation mechanisms of this persistent carbon pool, advancing our understanding of long-term carbon sequestration in the ocean.

presentations.presentation_title: Characterization of Oxygen Containing Functional Groups in Natural Organic Matter by FT-ICR-MS/MS
presentations.abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM), a major component of natural organic matter (NOM) plays a vital role in biogeochemical cycles across the land to ocean continuum influencing nutrient transport, metal complexation, and carbon sequestration. Across aquatic environments, DOM undergoes a spectrum of biotic and abiotic transformations that progressively modify its molecular composition, structure, and environmental reactivity. These transformations are strongly governed by oxygen-rich functional groups, which dictate molecular solubility, reactivity, and overall structural complexity ultimately shaping the fate and persistence of DOM. This study employs Fourier-transform ion cyclotron resonance tandem mass spectrometry (FT-ICR-MS/MS) combined with neutral loss (NL) dynamics (CO 2 , H 2 O, CO and CH 2 O) to elucidate the size-dependent distribution of oxygen-containing functional groups. Seven distinct DOM samples representing land to ocean continuum, were characterized across ~100 mass windows (200–900 m/z). MS/MS fragmentation revealed a consistent mass-dependent evolution of DOM structures. Low molecular-weight (LMW, <450 Da) molecules were dominated by aliphatic structures enriched in carboxyl and hydroxyl groups, exhibiting extensive fragmentation resembling carboxylate-rich alicyclic molecules (CRAM)-like structures. In contrast, high molecular-weight (HMW, >750 Da) molecules retained a large proportion of oxygen (~80% of total oxygen atoms) within stable aromatic or heteroatomic cores (e.g., phenol, ether, ester, and ketone), exhibiting lignin/tannin-like characteristics. These findings suggest molecular transition from oxygen-rich peripheral functionalities in LMW DOM to more condensed and recalcitrant core structures in HMW DOM. Moreover, carboxyl dynamics indicate that the intensity in FT-ICR-MS is not primarily governed by molecular abundance, as commonly assumed. Instead, carboxyl content plays a dominant role in determining ionization efficiency affecting the overall intensity. Overall, these insights provide in-depth insights into the structural diversity of DOM and improve our understanding of DOM reactivity, transformation, and persistence in natural environments with implications for ocean carbon sequestration and long-term carbon storage.

presentations.presentation_title: Experimental Evaluation of Factors Controlling Microbial Carbon Pump Efficiency: Roles of Temperature, Substrate Quality, Sediments, and Benthic Organisms
presentations.abstract: Microorganisms metabolize labile organic matter in aquatic environments, generating refractory dissolved organic matter (RDOM) as a metabolic byproduct, a portion of which is detectable as humic-like fluorescent DOM (FDOM-H). This process, known as the microbial carbon pump, has garnered significant attention as a mechanism for long-term sequestration of organic carbon in aquatic systems. In this study, we examined the influences of water temperature, substrate composition, sedimentary flux, and benthic organism activity on microbial carbon pump efficiency, as approximated by FDOM-H production efficiency, through long-term biodegradation experiments using organic matter in water, as well as incubation experiments with surface sediment cores. We utilized Lake Biwa (Japan), one of the hotspots of the microbial carbon pump, as a model site. Our results revealed that elevated water temperatures and reduced concentrations of semi-labile organic matter in the substrate facilitated enhanced FDOM-H production. Additionally, we observed a significant sedimentary flux of FDOM-H into the overlying water, with a further increase following the addition of benthic organisms. These findings highlight the sensitivity of the microbial carbon pump to environmental conditions in the water column and at the sediment–water interface, suggesting that environmental changes may impact its capacity for carbon sequestration.

presentations.presentation_title: Microplastic Contamination Enhances Benthic Dissolved Organic Carbon Fluxes and Molecular Transformations in Sediments
presentations.abstract: Microplastics (MPs) are pervasive in aquatic environments and ultimately accumulate in sediments, yet their role in regulating benthic carbon cycling remains poorly constrained, particularly with respect to dissolved organic matter (DOM) exchange across the sediment–water interface. In this study, we conducted 28-day laboratory sediment-column incubations under controlled oxic and hypoxic conditions to quantify MP-induced changes in DOM quantity and composition in porewater and overlying water. Polyethylene (PE; petroleum-based) and polylactic acid (PLA; bio-based) MPs were added at 5% (w/w) as a high-end (hotspot) loading scenario. MP contamination increased porewater dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations by up to 27-fold relative to controls, resulting in 1.6–18-fold higher cumulative benthic DOC fluxes across the sediment–water interface. Size-fractionation and fluorescence indices revealed polymer-specific shifts in exported DOM quality: PLA enhanced DOC fluxes enriched in low-molecular-weight neutral fractions, whereas PE induced more pronounced compositional restructuring of exported DOM. Molecular-level analyses showed that MPs substantially reshaped DOM composition, contributing up to one-third of all detected molecular features despite comprising only ~5% of sediment mass, indicating that MPs act both as direct DOM sources and as facilitators of sedimentary DOM mobilization and transformation. Oxygen availability strongly modulated these responses, with oxic conditions favoring microbially transformed, labile compounds and hypoxic conditions promoting the accumulation of more recalcitrant, MP-associated molecular signatures. A bounding, order-of-magnitude assessment suggests that localized MP hotspots may yield non-negligible DOC contributions beyond the sediment scale, while underscoring uncertainties associated with extrapolation to environmentally realistic MP distributions and redox regimes. Overall, these findings demonstrate that sediment-associated MPs can function as biogeochemically active agents that enhance benthic carbon fluxes and alter DOM molecular composition, with important implications for sediment–water carbon exchange in impacted aquatic systems.

presentations.presentation_title: A Chemical Space Refinement Framework for Decoding the Structural Complexity of Dissolved Organic Matter
presentations.abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) is ubiquitous across almost all environments, from waters and soils to the atmosphere, influencing processes ranging from the global carbon cycle to engineered systems. Yet its extreme structural complexity has hindered a mechanistic understanding of DOM reactivity and transformation. Here, we present a chemical space refinement framework that integrates ultra-high resolution Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR MS), tandem mass spectrometry (MS 2 ) analysis, and a multi-source network traversal (MSNT) algorithm to curate structurally coherent DOM assemblages beyond conventional molecular formula-based analysis. Starting from formula-level paired mass-difference network, MSNT propagates structural information from known seeds through structural-similarity connections to construct refined chemical space in which structural candidates serve as proxies for molecular motifs and physicochemical traits of DOM. Benchmarking this strategy against KEGG biotransformation network and lignin reference materials (a key terrestrial precursor) showed that MSNT-refined candidates retained consistency with database- or MS 2 -informed structures, and captured the photochemical transformation of lignin-derived DOM, including the emergence of high-polar carboxyl-rich alicyclic molecule (CRAM)-like and condensed aromatic structures. Applying the framework to global DOM materials and long-term incubation datasets (162 samples in total) further revealed that photochemical oxidation of riverine and terrestrial DOM reshapes chemical space toward convergent signatures resembling CRAM-like coastal DOM, primarily through dearomatization and carbonylation that probably proceed concurrently with structural diversification. The developed framework is transferable to other complex environmental mixtures, providing interpretable structural constraints on DOM reactivity and transformation across diverse environments.

presentations.presentation_title: NOM Data Are Compositional: And This Is Not Optional
presentations.abstract: Compositional data (CoDa) are ubiquitous in environmental research. They describe parts of a whole, including percentages, proportions, and relative or absolute abundances. Such data consist of positive values, where the essential information is contained in the ratios among components. Conventional statistical methods developed for real random variables often produce spurious results when applied to CoDa and are therefore inappropriate. This stems from the unique geometric property of CoDa, namely, their sample space is confined to a simplex rather than the real Euclidean space (e.g., CoDa with three parts can be represented inside a triangle). Notably, the simplex has one fewer dimension than the number of components. CoDa analysis has gained broad recognition across disciplines, from geosciences to social sciences, and has seen a recent rapid increase in use in microbial genomics. In contrast, its application in natural organic matter (NOM) research remains limited, even though data generated by major analytical techniques—such as mass spectrometry, fluorescence spectroscopy, and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy—are inherently compositional. Appropriate handling of CoDa is necessary for valid statistical inference when investigating factors affecting NOM dynamics. In this talk, I will walk through the application of CoDa analysis to NOM research, using ultrahigh-resolution mass spectrometry data of lacustrine dissolved organic matter as an illustrative example. The aim is to provide an accessible overview of CoDa concepts and offer practical guidance on their implementation for the NOM research community.

presentations.presentation_title: The Resilience Paradox: Widespread Greening Masks Critical Resilience Weakening in China's Ecosystems
presentations.abstract: Global vegetation greening is reshaping the terrestrial biosphere and is widely regarded as a signal of ecological improvement and enhanced ecosystem functioning. However, greening does not necessarily translate into higher ecosystem resilience, which is defined as the capacity to recover from disturbances, and may have a risk of resilience loss, increasing the likelihood of abrupt ecosystem transitions especially under ongoing climate change. Here, we assess the resilience of China’s terrestrial ecosystems over the past two decades by estimating recovery rates from the autocorrelation and variance of satellite-derived vegetation indicators. We find extensive greening (93.02% of the area), but nearly half (49.30%) of ecosystems exhibit significant resilience loss. This divergence produces a resilience paradox: among regions with significant trends in both greenness and resilience, almost half (48.10%) are greening yet losing resilience, indicating a widespread decoupling. Interpretable machine-learning and nonlinear sensitivity analyses show that water deficits, atmospheric drying, and intensifying drought are the primary drivers eroding resilience, particularly in fragile drylands, high-elevation regions, and ecosystems limited by shallow or coarse-textured soils. Moreover, short-rotation plantations and agroforestry systems exhibit persistent greening–resilience decoupling under both favorable and adverse climatic trends, likely due to structural and management constraints. Our findings reveal a hidden vulnerability within greening ecosystems and highlight the need to include resilience as a key component of climate adaptation and ecological restoration strategies in order to avoid future critical transitions.

presentations.presentation_title: Assessing Future Carbon Flux Variability in South Korean Riverine Wetlands: A CLM-FATES Modeling Approach
presentations.abstract: Wetland ecosystems represent one of the most dynamic yet vulnerable carbon reservoirs in the terrestrial biosphere. Given their significant role in global biogeochemical cycles, quantifying the carbon budget of riverine wetlands is imperative for predicting ecosystem responses to anthropogenic climate forcing. This study investigates the carbon exchange dynamics of riverine wetlands in South Korea, focusing on the sensitivity of these hydrologically active zones to shifting climatic regimes. To enhance predictive fidelity, we utilized the Community Land Model coupled with the Functionally Assembled Terrestrial Ecosystem Simulator (CLM-FATES). The modeling framework was driven by high-resolution spatio-temporal forcing datasets synthesized from PRISM and LDAPS, capturing the localized climatic variability essential for simulating wetland-specific processes. To address inherent model uncertainties, a robust stochastic calibration was performed: 1,000 parameter sets were generated via Latin Hypercube Sampling (LHS), and the model was constrained through Generalized Likelihood Uncertainty Estimation (GLUE) against empirical observations. By projecting optimized parameters onto future climate trajectories, this research quantifies the anticipated shifts in net ecosystem CO2 and CH4 exchange. The integration of high-resolution meteorological inputs and the GLUE-based uncertainty framework significantly improves the model's capacity to simulate complex vegetation-soil-atmosphere interactions in riverine environments. The findings elucidate the non-linear responses of carbon fluxes to temperature and precipitation anomalies, identifying potential thresholds for carbon sink-to-source transitions under future projections. Ultimately, this study provides a rigorous quantitative foundation for data-driven carbon management, offering scientific insights necessary for enhancing ecosystem resilience and formulating mitigation strategies in temperate wetland systems. presentations.presentation_title: Deep Learning Reveals a Weaker CMIP6 Terrestrial Carbon Sink with Reduced Uncertainty
presentations.institution: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
presentations.abstract: Terrestrial ecosystems have cumulatively sequestered 24% of anthropogenic carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions since 1850 and are critical for mitigating future climate change. However, current Earth System Models (ESMs) remain highly uncertain in projecting future trajectories of this carbon sink capacity, hampering our predictive understanding of climate mitigation potential and impeding effective climate and carbon management policies. This study develops a novel framework that harnesses deep-learning (DL) to constrain uncertainties of ESM-projected Gross Primary Production (GPP) and Net Ecosystem Production (NEP) through 2100. Specifically, we apply DL to characterize the “offset” between ESM-simulated output (using CMIP6 models) and best-available observational products (top-down, bottom-up). This offset is treated as unresolved processes by current ESMs that could be effectively resolved by DL, which, once trained during historical periods, can be applied to adjust CMIP6 projections of the future. We find that DL significantly reduces the inter-model spread of GPP by ~56% and NEP by ~66% across the CMIP6 ESM ensemble . Under the medium emission scenario (SSP 245), the ensemble mean for NEP in 2100 is much weaker, 2.42 ± 1.16 PgC yr -1 compared to 5.52 ± 3.45 PgC yr -1 in the raw CMIP6 projections, suggesting a current overestimation of future carbon sequestration capability. Interestingly, DL revealed a slower trajectory of NEP growth compared to the raw CMIP6 projection. Beyond curbing the uncertainties of CMIP6 projections, DL also captures key environmental sensitivities of carbon cycle processes such as CO 2 fertilization and sensitivity to warming. These findings demonstrate the power of DL in effectively curbing ESMs projection uncertainties and suggest that relying solely on natural terrestrial carbon sinks for climate mitigation is unlikely to slow down climate warming.

presentations.presentation_title: Quantification of Carbon Cycling and Yield in Korean Rice Paddies Using Knowledge-guided Machine Learning
presentations.abstract: In agroecosystems, reliable estimation of carbon cycling is essential to achieve net-zero or even carbon-negative targets. However, traditional process-based (PB) models, designed to simulate ecosystem carbon and yield dynamics, face limitations in scalability across regions, crops, and management regimes and entail high computational costs, while machine-learning (ML) models are constrained by limited large-scale training data and challenges in interpretability. To bridge this gap, Liu et al. (2024) developed a knowledge-guided machine learning (KGML) framework for carbon-cycling prediction, combining PB and ML strengths, and validated KGML in the U.S. Corn Belt (corn/soybean).This study applies KGML to Korean rice paddies to annually quantify carbon cycling and yield at the local administrative level (si-gun) across South Korea. Paddy systems differ from corn–soybean systems in that they involve flooding–drainage cycles, transplanting, tillage and harvests. Model training in KGML consists of PB-based pretraining followed by observation-based fine-tuning. As inputs, we integrate multi-year meteorological characteristics, static soil properties, crop-management information, and rigorously validated satellite-derived gross primary production (GPP) products to produce nationwide annual si–gun-level estimates. The KGML model is pretrained on synthetic trajectories simulated by the DeNitrification–DeComposition (DNDC) PB model and subsequently fine-tuned using eddy covariance (EC) flux tower measurements from Korean rice paddy fields. Generalization is evaluated using held-out EC flux tower observations, and results are reported as annual si–gun-level estimates and tabulated budgets of carbon cycling and yield.As a foundational step toward nationwide application, we evaluate the predictability and generalizability of KGML for Korean rice paddies to support robust annual si–gun-level quantification of carbon cycling and yield. presentations.presentation_title: Foscenes: a High-Fidelity, Large-Scale 3D Forest Scenes Dataset to Enhance Physics-informed Information Retrieval
presentations.abstract: Accurate three-dimensional (3D) representations of forest plant area density (PAD) are essential for characterizing canopy structure and providing realistic scene inputs for 3D radiative transfer models (RTMs) in remote sensing. However, existing lidar-based voxelization methods capable of resolving fine-scale PAD distributions are typically limited to small spatial extents, restricting their application in large-scale forest studies and the interpretation of Earth Observation Satellite (EOS) data. To address this limitation, we developed Large-Scale Path Volume Leaf Area Density (LS-PVlad), a novel reconstruction workflow that generates high-resolution (≤ 2 m) voxelized forest scenes over areas of up to 100 km² using globally available open-access airborne lidar scanning (ALS) data. Applying LS-PVlad to NASA Goddard’s LiDAR, Hyperspectral, and Thermal Imager (G-LiHT) campaigns, we produced FoScenes, a high-fidelity 3D PAD dataset comprising 40 forest scenes across 28 ecologically diverse sites worldwide, with individual areas ranging from approximately 50 to 11,000 ha. The PAD-derived leaf area estimates were validated using two years of field-measured leaf area index (LAI) from litter collection and digital hemispherical photography, achieving root mean square errors of 0.35 and 0.46 m²/m², respectively. By providing seamless, large-scale, and structurally realistic forest scenes at unprecedented spatial coverage and resolution, FoScenes enables simulations using 3D RTMs across a wide range of observation conditions and spatial scales. This can fill the data gap of real satellite observations caused by limited viewing angles, low revisiting frequency, and cloud contamination. Integrating such physics-based simulations into training datasets has the potential to increase the accuracy and robustness of deep-learning-based retrieval models. Furthermore, by providing necessary structure representation of real world for differentiable radiative transfer models (DRTMs), FoScenes can support the retrieval of vegetation optical properties and biochemical parameters, enable more accurate simulations and advance development of Forest Digital Twin (FDT) systems.

presentations.presentation_title: Brdf Correction and Validation of Land Surface Reflectance from Himawari-9/ahi Data
presentations.institution: Center for Environmental Remote Sensing (CEReS), Chiba University
presentations.abstract: Land surface reflectance is a critical parameter for terrestrial monitoring. To fully exploit Himawari-9/AHI (Advanced Himawari Imager) data, it is important to correct directional effects caused by land surface reflectance anisotropy. This correction usually requires semi-empirical Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) kernels. Although the Ross–Thick Li–Sparse–Reciprocal (RTK–LSR) model has been well validated for MODIS products, its applicability to geostationary satellite data is limited, particularly at high latitudes. In this study, two volume scattering kernels, Ross-Thick (RTK) and Ross-Thin (RTN), and three geometric scattering kernels, Li-Sparse-Reciprocal (LSR), Li-Dense (LDN), and Roujean (RJN) were used to determine the optimal BRDF kernel combination for Himawari-9/AHI data. The BRDF-adjusted reflectance from Himawari-9/AHI was normalized to the observation geometry of MODIS/Terra to enable further validation. Representative samples of different land cover types distributed across a range of latitudes over the full disk were selected to assess the performance of kernel combinations, with the MODIS MOD09GA surface reflectance product used as a reference for validation. The results indicate that the kernel combinations involving the LDN geometric kernel demonstrate superior performance over most land cover types, whereas the RTN-RJN kernel combination performs better over barren soil surfaces. This study optimizes the BRDF correction method for Himawari-9/AHI, advancing the accuracy of reflectance products for time-series analysis and climate monitoring.

presentations.presentation_title: Vegetation Structural Controls on Lidar Foliage Profiles and Waveforms Revealed by Geometric–optical Radiative Transfer Modeling
presentations.institution: Hunter College of The City University of New York
presentations.abstract: The Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) mission provides high-quality full-waveform lidar measurements of forest vertical structure in temperate and tropical forests between 51.6° N and S latitude. Beyond vegetation height metrics, GEDI waveforms contain information about vertical foliage distribution profiles. However, understanding which vegetation structure parameters most strongly influence these foliage profiles is essential for accurate waveform simulation and future parameter retrieval efforts.This study employs the Geometric Optical and Radiative Transfer (GORT) model to identify vegetation structure controls on lidar-derived foliage profiles and waveform characteristics. The GORT model directly links vegetation structure parameters—including tree geometry, crown dimensions, foliage volume density, tree count density, and tree height—to simulated foliage profiles and lidar waveforms. We compared two model implementations: the original multi-cohort version and an expanded individual tree-based version that incorporates tree-level structural variation.Using individual tree structure measurements collected from two National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) sites: TEAK (Lower Teakettle, conifer forest) and HARV (Harvard Forest, deciduous forest), we simulated foliage profiles and waveforms from observed tree structure data and validated them against small footprint lidar measurements. Modeled foliage profiles showed strong agreement with lidar-derived profiles, particularly for single-layer canopies. Both the multi-cohort and individual tree-based GORT models produced similar foliage profiles, suggesting model formulation is robust across scales.Sensitivity analysis reveals that beyond tree height and density, two architectural traits—crown shape and leaf arrangement—are critical parameters for accurate foliage profile simulation. Additionally, foliage volume density exhibits significant vertical and radial stratification within crowns, with higher densities concentrated in upper and outer crown layers. These findings identify key vegetation structure parameters required for accurate lidar waveform modeling and establish a foundation for future structure parameter retrieval from spaceborne lidar systems like GEDI.

presentations.presentation_title: An Automated Workflow for Extracting Land Surface Phenology from Phenocam Time‑lapse Images
presentations.abstract: Understanding land surface phenology is essential for tracking how ecosystems respond to climate change. PhenoCam systems are widely used for this purpose as they capture high-resolution imagery of seasonal plant growth. However, a major challenge in using these systems is the massive time-series data produced. Existing methods/tools rely on manual ROI selection and limited automation, slowing large-scale analysis. As a result, handling the large volume of imagery remains time-consuming and requires expert effort. To address these challenges, we developed PhenoAI. It's a Python framework that automates the entire PhenoCam data processing chain. The framework consists of four integrated modules: (i) automated image quality control, (ii) vegetation segmentation using an EfficientNet-B3 CNN model, (iii) automatic ROI generation via K-means clustering, and (iv) the extraction of phenological parameters. We validated this framework using a five-year dataset (2017–2021) consisting of 20,634 images of black spruce (Picea mariana) in Quebec, Canada. PhenoAI identified and filtered 28% of them as low-quality (foggy, snowy, dark, and blurred categories) with <94% accuracy under manual verification. The deep learning CNN model achieved an IoU of 87.3%, which provided accurate segmentation of vegetation from soil/background. The resulting greenness time-series showed a start of season near DOY 144 ± 5, peak greenness around DOY 183 ± 5, and an end of season near DOY 269 ± 20. These values align with previous studies at the same site, species and camera model and differ by only ±5 days for SOS and ±8 days for EOS. PhenoAI provides a validated and efficient workflow that removes the need for manual intervention. By simplifying data extraction, this tool enables researchers to better examine species-specific responses to climate variability across extensive camera networks. The workflow is open-source and produces phenology outputs that support ecological research and forest management.

presentations.presentation_title: Monitoring, Mapping, and Validating Land Surface Phenology Across Diverse Ecosystems
presentations.abstract: Land surface phenology (LSP) derived from satellite observations is a critical indicator of ecosystem responses to climate variability and change. However, widely used global LSP algorithms perform poorly in many climate-sensitive ecosystems where phenology is driven primarily by rainfall rather than temperature, and where vegetation greenness does not necessarily correspond to active photosynthesis. In such systems, conventional greenness-based approaches often fail to capture functionally meaningful phenological transitions under increasing climate extremes. To address these limitations, we developed a modified threshold-based phenology algorithm specifically designed for ecosystems where current methods break down. Recognising that traditionally used greenness indices such as the Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI) may be decoupled from ecosystem function, we integrated Global dataset of Solar-Induced chlorophyll Fluorescence (GOSIF) Gross Primary Productivity (GPP) with EVI to extract phenological metrics that better represent photosynthetic activity. This multi-source approach leverages emerging satellite products to link structural and functional vegetation dynamics. We derived key LSP metrics including the start, peak, end, and length of growing seasons, the minimum EVI value prior to and after the peak date, the seasonal maximum EVI value, the integral EVI value during the growing season, and seasonal amplitude. Application across diverse Australian climate zones demonstrated substantial improvements in phenology detection, particularly in arid and semi-arid shrublands and savannas, tropical and subtropical savannas, and temperate evergreen forests. Phenological metrics were retrieved for more than 74% of Australia, compared to less than 32% using an existing global LSP product. Phenology validation remains challenging and requires explicit protocols. We validated the phenological metrics against eddy covariance flux tower GPP, demonstrating that the approach reliably captures functionally meaningful phenology. By leveraging state-of-the-art satellite technologies, this work advances the capacity to monitor phenological responses to climate change and supports applications such as bushfire risk assessment and ecosystem carbon cycle analysis.
