presentations.presentation_title: Long-distance Lateral Export of Coastal Vegetation Sustains Deep-sea Carbon Sequestration in the South China Sea and the Northwestern Pacific
presentations.abstract: Long-distance lateral export can connect highly productive coastal vegetation to deep-sea carbon sinks, yet its sources and persistence remain difficult to verify at taxonomic resolution. Here we integrate eDNA metabarcoding (18S V9 rDNA) with stable isotopes (δ¹³C, δ¹⁵N) and organic-carbon metrics to trace coastal macrophyte signatures in offshore particles and deep sediments across the northern South China Sea (NSCS) and the subtropical northwestern Pacific margin. In the NSCS, particulate organic carbon collected at 500 m off southwestern Taiwan (Station T) and Dongsha Atoll (Station K) revealed contrasting exported sources: seagrass detritus predominated at Station K, whereas macroalgae-derived detritus dominated at Station T. The concordance of δ¹³C signatures between offshore particles and candidate macrophyte sources supports stable carbon isotopes as a practical indicator for tracking detached vegetation after transport and transformation. On the northwestern Pacific margin off Taiwan, a two-decade record (2001–2021) links rising sea-surface temperature and nutrient influx to the proliferation of climate-resilient macroalgae and their incorporation into deep-sea sediments. Outdoor experiments with Pterocladiella capillacea and Turbinaria ornata further indicate that nutrient enrichment strengthens resilience under warming and low salinity. eDNA barcoding, total organic carbon, and isotopic trends (increasing δ¹³C and δ¹⁵N, especially at greater depths) reveal selective deposition of key taxa and an increasingly macroalgal carbon signature in sedimentary organic matter. Together, paired water-column and sediment archives demonstrate that lateral export is a measurable coastal-to-deep sea conduit that can materially enhance deep-ocean carbon storage in the NSCS–northwestern Pacific system, and they provide an MRV-ready toolkit for resolving sources, transport, and sequestration outcomes.

presentations.presentation_title: Different Contributions of Climate Change and Anthropogenic Activities to Eutrophication of Rivers and Lakes in Asia’s Largest River Basin (yangtze River)
presentations.abstract: The impact of anthropogenic activities and climate change on surface water eutrophication has been of great concern. However, the contribution proportions of anthropogenic activities and climate change to the lakes and rivers’ eutrophication in large basins has not been clearly revealed. This study employed Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) and Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) to conduct a dual quantiffcation of the differential contributions of anthropogenic activities and climate change to the eutrophication of rivers and lakes in the Yangtze River Basin (YRB). Regression coefffcients of GWR variables demonstrated the spatial heteroge-neity of eutrophication drivers. Shapley additive explanations showed that nutrients and land use intensity were the main drivers during wet seasons. Combining the direct and indirect path results from SEM, the relative contribution of anthropogenic activities and climate change was 92.1 % and 7.9 % to river eutrophication, respectively, and was 67.1 % and 32.9 % to lake eutrophication, respectively. Anthropogenic activities consis-tently exacerbate eutrophication in both rivers and lakes, whereas climate change intensiffes lake eutrophication but exerts seasonally variable effects on rivers. These ffndings revealed that intensive anthropogenic activities continue to dominate the eutrophication of the YRB. This study can provide a scientiffc reference for the integrated management of aquatic ecosystems in large basins.

presentations.presentation_title: Measurement-based Evidence for Tier 3 GHG Accounting in Tropical Peatlands: Implications for MRV and NDCs
presentations.abstract: Nature-based solutions (NbS) are increasingly embedded in national mitigation strategies under the UNFCCC; however, their credibility depends on robust, transparent, and measurement-based greenhouse gas (GHG) accounting. Tropical peatlands in Southeast Asia are a major source of land-sector emissions and a critical component of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), yet current estimates remain highly uncertain due to reliance on indirect approaches and generic emission factors. Strengthening Tier 3 Measurement, Reporting and Verification systems is therefore essential to improve national GHG inventories and the integrity of mitigation claims. Since 2016, we have implemented an integrated, long-term program of ground-based GHG measurements across intact peat swamp forest, degraded peatland, and Acacia crassicarpa plantations within a single peat landscape in Sumatra, Indonesia. Net ecosystem exchanges of CO 2 and CH 4 are quantified using eddy-covariance systems, complemented by chamber-based measurements of soil N 2 O. The observation framework has expanded to include lateral carbon export via drainage water from rivers and canals. Our results show that contemporary GHG emissions from Acacia plantations on peat are lower than IPCC default emission factors and values currently applied in Indonesia’s Forest Reference Emission Level, and consistently lower than emissions from degraded peatlands under comparable hydrological conditions. These findings indicate that establishing managed plantations on already degraded peatlands can reduce long-term emissions relative to continued degradation, also conservation of intact peat swamp forests clearly confirms substantial and measurable avoided emissions. Overall, this study demonstrates how sustained, ground-based Tier 3 measurements can reduce uncertainty in land-sector GHG inventories, strengthen MRV systems, and support more credible mitigation accounting and claims for peatland-based nature-based solutions.

presentations.presentation_title: Ammonia Exchange Flux Measurements Over Vegetated Ecosystems in East Asia
presentations.abstract: Nitrogen is an essential element for human society and has greatly supported agricultural production and manufacturing. However, excessive nitrogen use imposes a heavy burden on the environment, contributing to climate change, air/water pollution, acidification, eutrophication, and biodiversity loss through atmospheric deposition. As a major component of reduced reactive nitrogen (Nr), ammonia (NH 3 ) has received increasing attention in recent years. East Asia is one of the regions at high risk of nitrogen pollution and a hotspot for nitrogen deposition. Recent studies have shown that the contribution of NH 3 dry deposition to total nitrogen deposition has increased significantly, following the dramatic reduction in nitrogen oxides emissions. However, these model-based estimates involve large uncertainties and the quantification of NH 3 deposition remains technically challenging in this region; NH 3 exhibits a complex behavior of bi-directional exchange as it not only deposits on the surface but is also emitted to the atmosphere via plants and soil. To clarify the characteristics of NH 3 bi-directional exchange and to contribute to a more accurate assessment of nitrogen deposition in East Asia, we have conducted NH 3 exchange flux measurements over forests, croplands, and grasslands in Japan since 2015. More recently, we also present the first observations of NH 3 exchange flux over a tropical dry deciduous forest in Thailand. We employed the aerodynamic gradient method and the relaxed eddy accumulation method for flux measurements. The observed fluxes mostly fall within the range reported in previous studies in other regions, suggesting that NH 3 bi-directional exchange in East Asia is comparable to that in Europe and North America. Although we applied a bi-directional exchange model to interpret the observation results, the performance was not satisfactory, indicating the need for further improvement. Future studies should incorporate state-of-the-art measurement technologies in addition to detailed analyses of plant and soil parameters.

presentations.presentation_title: Spatially-resolved Co2 and H2o Fluxes from an Agricultural System Using a Next-generation Eddy Covariance Platform
presentations.abstract: Growing interest in carbon sequestration and climate-smart land management is driving demand for scalable, defensible measurements of ecosystem-scale carbon and water fluxes. Eddy covariance (EC) is a core method for directly quantifying surface-atmosphere exchanges of greenhouse gases, water, and energy.Globally scaling these direct measurements requires instrument and analytic solutions that reduce costs, power consumption, and complexity, without compromising data accuracy, quality, or confidence. It also requires integration with other biophysical data sources - such as biomass inventories, remote sensing, and land-atmosphere models.The Carbon Node was purpose-built to overcome these challenges. Powered by the LI-720 CO₂/H₂O flux sensor, it delivers eddy covariance-quality results with significantly lower cost, maintenance, and power requirements, making high-quality flux measurements accessible to a broader user base.Combining the Internet of Things with environmental science enables edge and cloud computing to create a seamless data pipeline that converts raw sensor outputs into analysis-ready data, with processing occurring both on-sensor and in the cloud, where computing capacity is less constrained. This Internet of the Environment (IoE) approach utilizes higher spatial measurement density, improving representation of global spatial heterogeneity.These systems stream real-time flux data to a cloud-based platform with automated processing, quality control, and analysis. A spatialized eddy covariance method (FluxMapper™) further resolves surface flux contributions at sub-hourly temporal and decameter spatial scales. The resulting high-resolution, geotagged flux maps more effectively link flux observations with remote sensing, providing a streamlined end-to-end CO₂/H₂O flux solution.We present results from a field experiment combining traditional EC towers with a distributed network of Carbon Nodes to assess spatial heterogeneity in CO₂ and latent heat fluxes across a working agricultural field. Distributed measurements reveal diurnal patterns in carbon uptake and evapotranspiration associated with soil moisture gradients, management practices, and crop development.

presentations.presentation_title: Redwoods Forest Flux Measurements for Societal Benefits
presentations.abstract: Coastal redwood forests are among California’s most productive and largest carbon-storing natural ecosystems. A gap in knowledge remains regarding their water and carbon fluxes due to the lack of direct flux measurements. In collaboration with multiple State agencies, we established two tall flux towers. The suite of measurements consists of more than 100 real-time variables to examine forest metabolism responses under varying fog conditions, different forest floor management practices, increasing drought, and other environmental change threats during a period when the State is preparing to achieve carbon neutrality by 2045. Our presentation will introduce our experiment, initial data collection, and potential challenges and opportunities for complex terrain science coupled with tall canopies. Study results will be uploaded to AmeriFlux and regularly communicated to State agencies, an advisory board, and local communities through meetings and cooperative extension events to obtain direct feedback on societal benefits. We invite suggestions for collaboration to continue this project beyond the current timeline for long-term study and broader impact.

presentations.presentation_title: Beyond Methane: Reassessing the Role of Rice Paddies in Global Warming
presentations.abstract: As a major cereal crop, the global demand for rice continues to increase. However, the expansion of rice cultivation is constrained by substantial methane (CH 4 ) emissions during flooded rice cultivation. Since various soil management practices have been developed to mitigate CH 4 emissions, and rice paddies have high potential for soil carbon (C) sequestration, the impact of rice cropping systems on global warming requires re-evaluation. To compare the effects of cropping on global warming between rice paddy and maize upland systems, the net global warming potential (GWP) was evaluated by integrating CH₄ and nitrous oxide (N₂O) fluxes and changes in soil organic C (SOC) stocks under identical fertilization regimes. During crop cultivation, net GWP in rice paddies was predominantly driven by CH₄ flux, whereas in upland fields it was strongly influenced by SOC stock depletion. Under conventional fertilization (NPK and green manure), net GWP was substantially higher in rice paddies than in upland systems; however, under biochar application, the climatic impact was markedly lower. Moreover, the combined application of CH 4 mitigation practices, including mid-season drainage, reduced the net GWP of paddy fields to levels considerably lower than those observed in upland fields. A similar trend was observed for greenhouse gas intensity (GHGI), which indicates the net GWP per grain productivity. Consequently, if CH₄ mitigation practices for rice paddies are effectively implemented, rice could be produced in a more climate-friendly manner than in upland systems.

presentations.presentation_title: Global Warming Decreased Soil Organic Carbon Stock Via Increasing Organic Matter Lability and Heterotrophic Respiration
presentations.abstract: Global warming can simultaneously increase plant net primary production (NPP) as a carbon (C) input and microbial decomposition of organic matter as a C output, making it challenging to predict its overall impact on soil organic C (SOC) accumulation. To evaluate the effects of global warming on SOC dynamics in paddy soils, current and projected climate conditions were simulated using Open Top Chambers. In the future climate scenario, atmospheric temperature and CO₂ concentration were elevated by 2 °C and 200 ppmV, respectively. Chemical or organic fertilizer treatments were added in both climate conditions. In the organic fertilizer plots, cover crops were cultivated during the cold fallow season and fully incorporated as green manure before rice transplanting. Changes in SOC stock during the cropping period were assessed using a net ecosystem C budget analysis, representing the balance between C inputs and outputs. Global warming reduced rice NPP by 9–20% under the same fertilization, while increasing microbial decomposition of organic matter by 28–98%. It also substantially increased dissolved organic matter in the soil without discriminating against chemical composition, further enhancing microbial decomposition. Consequently, SOC accumulation was markedly decreased under future climate conditions. While the cultivation and incorporation of cover crops increased SOC under current climate conditions, this practice was insufficient to enhance SOC accumulation under projected future climates. Overall, under future climate conditions, larger amounts of organic amendments may be required to achieve meaningful increases in SOC storage.

presentations.presentation_title: Process-guided and Al-assisted Soil Carbon Foundation Model for Natural Climate Solutions
presentations.abstract: Rapid greenhouse gas emission reductions and carbon dioxide removal (CDR) are essential to avoid the most dangerous climate impacts this century. The global soil system, which stores the largest amount of carbon in the biosphere, has immense potential for carbon sequestration—small fractional increases in soil carbon storage could lead to substantial carbon removal. However, verifiable and scalable solutions for promoting soil carbon storage to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere remain elusive. This presentation introduces a process-guided and AI-assisted modeling platform to verify durable CDR across local to global soils. This approach integrates state-of-the-art mechanistic models that simulate soil organic carbon and inorganic carbon dynamics with a scientifically interpretable reasoning AI algorithm, leveraging global observational datasets. Three key applications will be highlighted. First, we found microbial physiology as the first-order factor in regulating global soil organic carbon storage in shallow layers. Second, we showed redirecting plant carbon input into deep layers is an effective approach to promote deep soil carbon sequestration. Third, we quantified the CDR potential of enhanced rock weathering, a method introducing finely crushed silicate minerals to agricultural soils to sequester CO2 into stable carbonate, as a function of climate, soil biogeochemistry, and land management across global croplands. By bridging AI, mechanistic modeling, and big data, this framework supports science-backed verification and certification of soil-based natural climate solutions, enabling informed decision-making from local land management to global policy.

presentations.presentation_title: Climate and Topography Determine the Spatial Heterogeneity of Soil Organic Carbon Stocks Across Sri Lanka
presentations.abstract: Under recommended management practices soils can act as a sink for atmospheric carbon. Understanding the drivers of soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks at national scales is essential for effectively harnessing the sequestration potential and informing spatially targeted conservation policies. Here, we present a high-resolution assessment of SOC stocks across the Island of Sri Lanka (65,610 km²) based on an intensive field sampling campaign. A total of 1,488 surface soil samples (0–30 cm) were collected to represent the island’s climatic, topographic, and land-use variability and analyzed for SOC concentration, bulk density, and gravel content. Thirty-eight candidate spatial predictors describing topography, climate, vegetation, land use, and soil properties were compiled from digital spatial datasets. Machine-learning models were applied to quantify multivariate relationships between SOC stocks and environmental drivers, and Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) were used to evaluate the marginal contribution of individual predictors. SOC stocks exhibited pronounced spatial heterogeneity, ranging from 0.5 to 24.8 kg m⁻². Independent validation (n = 298) identified the random forest model as the best performer (R² = 0.51; RMSE = 2.36 kg m⁻²). SHAP analyses revealed climate, relief, and spatial position as the dominant controls on SOC distribution, with climate exerting the strongest influence. The aridity index emerged as the most important predictor, followed by annual precipitation, warmest-quarter precipitation, and potential evapotranspiration. Spatial patterns of SOC stocks reflected strong interactions between climatic gradients and topographic features. Overall, this sampling-intensive, data-driven analysis demonstrates that SOC stocks in Sri Lanka’s tropical soilscapes are highly heterogeneous and primarily structured by climate and topographic controls, providing a robust basis for national-scale carbon management and conservation planning.

presentations.presentation_title: Past and Present Hydrothermal Regimes Shape Microbial Resource Allocation for Soil C, N, and P Cycling and Its Attribution to Soil Carbon Dynamics Across the Continental United States
presentations.abstract: Understanding and predicting the feedback between climate change and soil carbon dynamics remains a major scientific challenge. A key uncertainty lies in our limited knowledge of how changing hydrothermal conditions influence microbial functional dynamics and their contributions to soil carbon emissions. In particular, the microbial functions that respond to hydrothermal variability—and their interactions with functions involved in soil carbon and nutrient cycling—remain poorly characterized. It is still unclear how both historical and current hydrothermal conditions affect the relative abundances of these microbial functions and how these shifts impact the dynamics of soil carbon emission in response to changing hydroclimate. To fill these knowledge gaps, we combined gene-to-ecosystem data from major ecological networks to develop artificial intelligence models to identify and quantify microbial resource allocation strategies in response to past and present hydrothermal properties. We further developed an explainable AI-Earth system model to assess how these microbial functions respond to historical and current hydrothermal conditions and to quantify their contributions to soil carbon dynamics. Our findings indicated that microbial communities acclimated to reduced soil moisture by lowering investment in recalcitrant-C decomposition and monomer nutrient mineralization. This drought-mitigation response was amplified by drying legacy but dampened by nutrient limitation. Elevated soil temperature, in contrast, generally increased microbial investment in N acquisition, while thermal legacy strengthened the thermal resistance of N-acquisition allocation and promoted reallocation of C- and P-acquiring functions toward adaptation to current hydrothermal dynamics. These hydrothermal regulations on microbial functions explain the spatiotemporal variability in soil carbon emissions observed across the conterminous United States (CONUS).

presentations.presentation_title: Coupled Carbon–water Dynamics Across Agroecosystems: Insights from Eddy-covariance Flux Towers
presentations.abstract: Understanding the coupled dynamics, which refers to the interdependent and coordinated variability of carbon and water fluxes, is essential for improving predictions of land–atmosphere feedback and crop yield. This study uses observations from eight eddy covariance flux towers installed across crop and pasture agroecosystems to quantify the coupled dynamics of Net Ecosystem Exchange (NEE), Gross Primary Productivity (GPP), Evapotranspiration (ET), and soil moisture. Correlation metrics and partial-correlation techniques were applied to isolate carbon–water interactions. This study also identifies the biometeorological controls that determine carbon-water coupling. Results reveal pronounced seasonal variability and strong statistical coupling between GPP and NEE, with ET, reflecting coordinated physiological regulation of photosynthesis and transpiration. Partial correlation analysis revealed a significant coupling between carbon and water fluxes. After controlling for soil moisture, evapotranspiration remained strongly positively correlated with GPP (0.91) and negatively correlated with NEE (-0.72). However, no strong copattern was detected between GPP and NEE with soil moisture. Controlling evapotranspiration, soil moisture poorly correlated with GPP (0.20) and NEE (0.16). Carbon–water coupling persists after controlling for energy-related variables, including latent heat flux, soil heat flux, and radiation, highlighting ecohydrological linkages. Comparisons between crop and pasture agroecosystems show differences in the magnitude and variability of carbon-water coupling. These findings demonstrate the value of integrated statistical analyses of eddy covariance measurements for advancing process-level understanding of carbon–water interactions in agroecosystems and for improving representation of managed landscapes in land surface and ecosystem models.

presentations.presentation_title: Augmenting the Inaccessible: a Gan-based Generative Framework for Advancing Soc Data–model Integration for High-latitude Regions
presentations.abstract: Soil organic carbon (SOC) is a fundamental driver of ecosystem resilience and nutrient cycling, yet its dynamics remain difficult to predict in high-latitude regions due to severe data fragmentation. While there is a need to integrate multi-source datasets into process-based models, circumpolar regions often lack the "ground truth" necessary for such scaling. This study addresses these critical knowledge gaps by introducing a generative AI framework that utilizes Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for creating real-world mimicking synthetic datasets, aiming to reduce uncertainties in SOC stock predictions to advance data–model integration.We utilize GenAI based digital twins of closely matched SOC profiles to synthesize high-fidelity datasets where field observations are logistically constrained. By classifying soil samples through key environmental drivers; including biome, soil type, and climate variables; we generate synthetic profiles that can be integrated into geospatial and statistical models. This approach was rigorously validated against abundant datasets from the continental USA to ensure the reliability of the GenAI in mimicking real-world SOC turnover and storage patterns.By creating extensive, high-resolution datasets of soil organic carbon profiles, this work provides a scalable solution to bridge the gap between plot-level observations and regional Earth system contexts. Presented method showcases novel path to reducing uncertainties in SOC feedbacks under changing climate regimes, offering a novel pathway to enhance predictive modeling and secure soil health in vulnerable, data-limited ecosystems. Additionally, this research signifies a paradigm shift in soil informatics by demonstrating that generative AI can overcome the “data desert” of remote ecosystems, transforming sparse field observations into robust, model-ready datasets that reduce global carbon cycle uncertainties.

presentations.presentation_title: Constraining Soil Organic Carbon Stocks in Southeast Asia Using Observations and Cmip6 Models
presentations.abstract: Soil organic carbon (SOC) is a fundamental ecosystem property that regulates the global carbon cycle and determines multiple ecosystem services critical to human well-being. Despite its importance, substantial uncertainties persist in estimates of SOC stocks and their controlling factors across Southeast Asia (SEA), a region characterized by strong climatic gradients, diverse land use, and limited soil profile observations. Here, we synthesized existing global SOC stock datasets, projections from Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) Earth system models (ESMs), existing soil profile observations, and spatially explicit environmental covariates to: (i) assess the current state of knowledge of SOC stocks in the SEA region, (ii) generate a new observation-constrained estimate of SOC stocks to quantify their magnitude, spatial distribution, and associated uncertainties, and (iii) identify the dominant environmental controls governing SOC variability across the region. Comparisons between observation-based SOC estimates and CMIP6 ESM representations reveal large discrepancies, indicating substantial uncertainties in the simulation of SOC stocks in SEA by current ESMs. The newly derived SOC stock estimates and their environmental drivers provide an improved benchmark for evaluating model performance and advancing regional carbon-cycle assessments. These results will be presented at the conference.

presentations.presentation_title: Woody Biochar Enhances Soil Carbon Stocks by Increasing Particulate Organic Matter Rather Than Mineral-associated Organic Matter in a Pepper Field
presentations.abstract: Woody biochar (WB) application is a promising strategy to enhance soil carbon (C) sequestration. Soil organic C stability is closely linked to its partitioning between particulate organic matter (POM) and mineral-associated organic matter (MAOM). However, few studies have evaluated how soil C sequestration mechanisms differ with WB application level. WB has been incorporated every year as basal fertilizer for 3 years under the different application levels (0, 2.5, 5 and 10 Mg ha -1 based on dry weight) under the recommended inorganic fertilization. We evaluated changes in soil C stocks in the surface soil (0-15 cm) by measuring bulk density and C content separately in the 0-5 and 5-15 cm layers. Then, SOM was physically fractionated following a size- and density-based approach into POM [light fraction (LF) and sand-size fraction] and MAOM [silt- and clay-sized fraction]. C and nitrogen (N) contents of each fraction were measured. Our results showed soil C stocks in surface soil significantly increased with increasing WB application levels, with the highest soil C stocks observed at WB10 (55.8 Mg C ha -1 ). The proportion of the LF increased progressively with increasing WB application levels, from 1.3% in WB0 to 3.1% in WB10. The contribution of POM-C to total SOC increased with WB application levels and showed the highest proportion in WB10 (46.1%). Accordingly, the POM-C/MAOM-C ratio increased significantly with WB application rate, suggesting a progressive limitation in the additional C sequestration capacity of MAOM. Furthermore, the MAOM index (MAOM per unit C input), declined markedly from 0.44 in WB2.5 to 0.07 in WB10, demonstrating a sharp decrease in MAOM-associated C accumulation efficiency with increasing WB application level. This study suggests that soil C sequestration becomes increasingly dependent on POM accumulation as WB application increases, and the additional C sequestration capacity of MAOM may be limited.

presentations.presentation_title: Residual Root-derived Carbon Influences Post-season Methane Emissions Under Different Rice Transplanting Dates in a Mono-rice Paddy Field
presentations.abstract: Adjusting rice transplanting dates affects crop growth and biomass production by changing meteorological conditions and the duration of flooding, strongly influencing methane (CH 4 ) emissions particularly in mono-rice paddy systems. After rice harvest, residual root biomass persists in the soil and can act as an important carbon (C) substrate for methanogens; however, how transplanting dates influence the quantity and characteristics of these root residues and their subsequent roles in regulating post-season CH₄ emissions remains poorly understood. We conducted a three-year field experiment (2022–2024) with two rice cultivars (early- and late-maturing) transplanted on four dates: May 10 (T1), May 25 (T2; locally recommended), June 9 (T3), and June 24 (T4). CH₄ fluxes were measured by static chamber method during rice cultivation, while root biomass and its chemical properties at rice harvest were analyzed to assess their roles in regulating CH 4 emissions in the following rice season. Regardless of cultivar and year, CH₄ emissions peaked at the earliest transplanting date (T1) and declined significantly (by 24–87%) with delayed transplanting during the rice cropping season. Root biomass at rice harvest decreased consistently with delayed transplanting across cultivars and years, changing in its chemical properties including C and nitrogen (N) composition, which potentially affects decomposition rates in the paddy soils. Notably, the potential C input from residual roots showed a strong positive correlation with CH₄ emissions in the following cropping season, indicating that residual root-derived C plays a critical role in regulating post-season CH₄ emissions in the mono-rice paddies. Overall, our findings provide new insight that bith the quantity and quality of residual root biomass remaining after the harvest should be considered key contributors to potentially influence CH₄ emissions during the following cropping seasons in a mono-rice paddy.

presentations.presentation_title: Mercury Emission Dynamics in India: Insights from Sensitivity Analysis
presentations.abstract: India, as the second-largest global emitter of mercury, faces significant environmental challenges despite being a signatory to the Minamata Convention. Mercury’s toxic nature, coupled with its long-lasting presence and tendencies to bioaccumulate and biomagnify, underscores the urgency of monitoring its emissions and impacts. However, India lacks robust ground-based observation data to assess mercury's distribution and deposition comprehensively. In this study, we utilized the GEOS-Chem model with the latest inventory available at 0.25° × 0.3125° to simulate mercury dynamics over India (2015 to 2017). The results reveal that regions hosting coal-based thermal power plants and brick kilns exhibit the highest mercury deposition (60-80 g km -2 a -1 ) and atmospheric concentrations (4-5 ng m -3 ). Sensitivity analyses delineated that Indian anthropogenic emissions contribute the largest share (~45%) to India’s mercury burden, exceeding the combined influence of natural + background sources (<30%) and Asian transboundary inputs (~30%), highlighting the dominant role of domestic emissions in regional mercury loading. This study provides insights into the spatial dynamics of mercury in India and highlights the regional interdependence of emissions. The study findings can guide policymakers in formulating targeted mitigation strategies to reduce mercury emissions and their transboundary impacts effectively. Further research is needed to examine the transformation of deposited mercury into its bioaccumulative form, methylmercury, and its implications for human health.

presentations.presentation_title: Zn Isotopic Composition And Variability In Large-scale Aquatic Environment Of The Tibetan Plateau: Implications For Zn Migration And Sources
presentations.abstract: In this investigation, we conducted extensive sampling of surface waters (including both upstream and downstream locations) to analyze Zn content and isotopic compositions (δ⁶⁶Zn). Our findings reveal that Tibetan Plateau (TP) surface waters are characterized by an enrichment of isotopically heavy Zn, with δ⁶⁶Zn ranging from 0.15 ± 0.01 ‰ to 0.49 ± 0.01 ‰. A notable distinction was observed between upstream (mean: 0.33 ± 0.09 ‰) and downstream samples (mean: 0.23 ± 0.03 ‰). While median Zn concentrations were comparable between the two sample types (upstream 1.49 μg L −1 ; downstream 1.89 μg L −1 ), this similarity is attributed to dilution effects from runoff convergence and the extensive sampling area. The correlation between EF Zn and Sc content, coupled with the similarity of δ⁶⁶Zn between glacier terminus waters and cryoconite across the TP, suggests anthropogenic influence on the aquatic environment, and the impact of glacier melting should not be ignored. Suspended particulate matter (SPM)-dominated samples exhibited higher Zn concentrations and δ⁶⁶Zn close to BSE value, indicating SPM may exert an influence on Zn fractionation. Zn fractionation in the cryospheric watershed appears to be shaped by multiple geochemical processes, including mineral adsorption, biological processes with grassland and permafrost vegetation as well as phytoplankton. In downstream areas, geochemical processes (mineral adsorption dominated), together with the substantial input of particles, appear to maintain δ⁶⁶Zn near the BSE, reflecting a shift from anthropogenic to natural significant. MixSIAR model simulations quantified the contributions to Zn in TP upstream watersheds as follows: glacial meltwater (29.2 %), geological input (42.3 %), traffic emissions (28.5 %).

presentations.presentation_title: Congener Specific Sequestration of Polychlorinated Biphenyls in the Global Ocean
presentations.abstract: The global ocean plays a crucial role in regulating the long-term fate of legacy persistent organic pollutants (POPs) such as Polychlorinated Biphenyls (PCBs). The behavior of PCBs in the atmosphere and surface oceans has been extensively studied. However their sequestration and transport in the deep ocean are still not well quantified, limiting our understanding of their long-term distribution in the marine environment. In this study, we extend the widely used global multimedia fate and transport model BETR-Global to explicitly represent oceanic depths down to 6000 m. Model simulations were performed from 1930 to 2024 for two representative congeners of PCB, PCB-28 and PCB-153. Modeled concentrations compare favorably with available observations in both surface and deep ocean waters. The simulations indicate a strong congener specific vertical distribution. PCB-28 is largely retained in surface waters, with 82.5% of its total oceanic inventory residing within the mixed layer and only about 4.4% transported to depths below 1000 m. In contrast, PCB-153 shows substantial accumulation in the deep ocean, with more than two-thirds of its total oceanic burden (approx 71.1%) stored below 1000 m. These results demonstrate that deep ocean waters act as a long-term, congener dependent sink for PCBs and play an important role in controlling their global residence times. Explicitly accounting for deep-ocean sequestration is therefore essential for improving global assessments of PCB persistence, re-emission to surface waters, and long-term exposure risks.

presentations.presentation_title: Oreochromis Niloticus and Anas platyrhynchos as bioindicators of microplastics and metal pollution in Ramsar Site, Central Mexico
presentations.institution: Universidad Popular Autónoma del Estado de Puebla
presentations.abstract: Fifteen Oreochromis niloticus (Tilapia) fish and 22 individuals of Anas platyrhynchos f. domesticus (domestic ducks) were collected in the Manuel Ávila Camacho (Valsequillo) dam in the area after the macrophyte consortium to investigate the presence of microplastics in their digestive system and trace element in liver, muscle, feathers, and blood. The determination of microplastics was made through a difference in densities finding in all of them fibers mainly, which were characterized by a field emission scanning electron microscope (FSEM).Performing muscle and liver analysis of the same fish, Zn> Cu> Mn> Cr> Ba> Ni> Pb> Hg> As> Co> Cd> Mo and Zn> Cu> Mn> Cr> Ni were found > Ba> Pb> Mo> Co> Hg> As> Cd respectively exceeding the international and national standards recommended for human consumption in both for Mn, Cr, Cu and Zn. On the other hand, the ducks results indicated high variability in element concentrations (CV > 36%), with the exception of copper in feathers, suggesting a significant degree of exogenous contamination resulting from anthropogenic activities.This study provides information on the consequences of pollution levels in the basin, where the dam, as the last part of the basin, functions as a pollutant receptor and artificial wetland. However, it visualizes the need for public policies that address the complex problem and comprehensive sanitation for the benefit of those who inhabit it.

presentations.presentation_title: Comparative Assessment of Mercury and Methylmercury in Korean Reservoirs and Rivers Based on the Survey Results of the National Monitoring Network
presentations.institution: Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: This study presents results from the National Mercury Integrated Monitoring Network (2016–2025) to evaluate progress under the Minamata Convention. Water, sediment, and fish samples were collected quarterly from five reservoirs (Okjeong, Buan, Chungju, Paro, and Paldang) and four downstream rivers (Geum, Nakdong, Yeongsan, and Han), and mercury (Hg) species were compared between reservoirs and rivers. In water, total mercury (THg) was higher in rivers (1.1±0.79 ng/L) than in reservoirs (0.62±0.36 ng/L), consistent with higher suspended particulate matter (SPM) in rivers, whereas filtered MeHg was higher in reservoirs (24±15 pg/L) than in rivers (22±10 pg/L). In sediment, both THg and MeHg were higher in reservoirs (97±95 and 0.70±0.68 μg/kg) than in rivers (40±31 and 0.18±0.23 μg/kg), consistent with longer water residence times in reservoirs. Overall, 96% of fish samples were below the international guideline for THg (<500 μg/kg); fish THg was higher in reservoirs (180±200 μg/kg) than in rivers (54±48 μg/kg), consistent with sediment Hg. Pearson correlations showed positive relationships between chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) and MeHg in reservoirs (r = 0.55, n = 330) and between SPM and MeHg in rivers (r = 0.30, n = 288), suggesting in situ MeHg production in reservoirs and greater ex situ influence in rivers. Principal component analysis supported these patterns, with Chl-a and SPM identified as key factors for MeHg in reservoir and river waters, respectively. Mann–Kendall tests showed significant decreases in MeHg at most sites from 2016 to 2025; the declines may be related to (i) reduced primary production, (ii) shifts in oxygen regime, and (iii) changes in dissolved organic carbon, potentially lowering net methylation and/or enhancing removal. Overall, these survey results support the evaluation of long-term changes in mercury in freshwater ecosystems in South Korea under the Minamata Convention.

presentations.presentation_title: Isolating the Effect of Elevated CO2 on GPP Based on 20-year Eddy Covariance Fluxes and SVAT Model in a Seasonal Tropical Rainforests
presentations.institution: Xishuangbanna Tropical Garden, China Academy of Science
presentations.abstract: Over the past two decades, a tropical seasonal rainforest at the northern edge of Southeast Asia has exhibited increasing gross primary production (GPP) alongside rising atmospheric CO₂ concentration ([CO₂]). The CO 2 sink increased from 128.3 g C m −2 yr −1 for the first decade to 187.5 g C m −2 yr −1 for the second decade; in the meantime, GPP increased from 2505.7 C m −2 yr −1 for the first decade to 2810.6 g C m −2 yr −1 for the second decade. To quantify the independent direct contribution of elevated [CO₂] to interannual carbon dynamics, we applied a multilayer soil–vegetation–atmosphere transfer (SVAT) model to 20 years of eddy covariance flux data. By controlling [CO₂] and using photosynthetic parameter Vcmax as a proxy index in model simulations, we isolated the CO₂ effect (driven by [CO₂] increase) from the non-CO₂ effect (driven by variations in temperature, radiation, and moisture). Critically, CO 2 effect averagely contribute to 6.2% of the interannual GPP. The CO₂ effect not only compensates for negative impacts from climatic stressors but also closely matches the magnitude of the interannual atmospheric carbon sink (net ecosystem exchange). This demonstrates that elevated [CO₂] has been essential in maintaining the carbon sink strength of this seasonal rainforest by counteracting moisture-related limitations and sustaining GPP enhancement under favorable light conditions. Our findings underscore the vital role of elevated [CO₂] in stabilizing the carbon sink in tropical marginal forests under changing climate and highlight its potential influence in the coming decades.

presentations.presentation_title: Vegetation shifts drive drought-induced changes in carbon, water, and energy dynamics in a savanna ecosystem
presentations.institution: Xishuangbanna Tropical Botanical Garden, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: Increasing drought frequency and intensity affect biophysical functions of natural ecosystems. In tropical semi-arid savannas, while immediate drought effects are well-studied, the drought legacy effects on vegetation composition and associated ecosystem functions remain unclear. We used data of vegetation composition, net ecosystem CO 2 exchange, surface albedo, and evapotranspiration (ET) in 2017–2022 from a savanna ecosystem, Southwest China, to investigate the legacy effect of an extreme drought event that occurred in 2019. Vegetation declined continuously for 3 post-drought years. While tree numbers declined by 12%, shrub numbers dropped by 50% compared with pre-drought levels, shifting vegetation dominance toward trees. This structural change caused sustained reductions in albedo and ET, which remained below pre-drought levels, despite that gross primary production recovered in the years immediately post-drought. Vegetation shifts disproportionately impact ecosystem functions, with energy and water fluxes exhibiting greater vulnerability and potentially enhancing regional warming as droughts increase in Asian savannas.

presentations.presentation_title: Bharat GPP: a Network-calibrated Gross Primary Productivity Dataset for India (2001–2025)
presentations.abstract: Gross primary productivity (GPP) underpins assessments of terrestrial carbon uptake, ecosystem functioning, and agricultural productivity. In India, croplands and forests together account for over 80% of the land surface and are strongly shaped by anthropogenic management and environmental changes. The absence of a nationally calibrated GPP dataset has consequently limited the reliable characterisation of land–atmosphere carbon exchange processes. The existing GPP products rely on global parameterisation, lacking direct calibration with local flux measurements, and thus struggle to represent India's diverse and heterogeneous landscapes. Here we present Bharat GPP, the first network-calibrated GPP dataset for India, providing daily estimates at 500 m spatial resolution for the period 2001–2025. Bharat GPP is built on a two-leaf light-use efficiency framework and calibrated using more than 30 site-years of eddy covariance observations from 26 flux towers spanning India's major biomes. Site-level evaluation shows strong performance across natural vegetation (R² mean = 0.45 ± 0.19, RMSE mean = 2.18 ± 1.18 gC/m 2 /day) and reasonable accuracy in heterogeneous croplands (R² mean = 0.32 ± 0.20, RMSE mean =2.55 ± 0.80 gC/m 2 /day) at the daily scale, outperforming the widely used MODIS GPP product. Sensitivity analyses across multiple meteorological forcings and vegetation indices indicate that model performance is primarily governed by canopy representation. To upscale site-level calibration to a sub-continental scale, we implement a plant functional type-based framework with a cropland stratification strategy combining aridity indices and solar-induced fluorescence-derived phenological timing. For croplands, our results are evaluated against an independent, structurally calibrated GPP dataset derived from district-level crop yield statistics. Bharat GPP provides a process-constrained baseline for monitoring carbon dynamics in Indian landscapes and offers a transferable framework for developing regionally calibrated GPP products in other data-scarce regions.

presentations.presentation_title: Integrated Monitoring of the Terrestrial Carbon Cycle Across Asia Based on Multiple Bottom-up Approaches
presentations.abstract: Asia has experienced rapid land-use changes driven by accelerated economic development, together with pronounced impacts of climate change. In this study, we assessed the terrestrial CO₂ budget across Asia since 2000 by synthesizing multiple bottom-up estimation approaches. These approaches include process-based ecosystem models, remote sensing–driven models, and data-driven upscaling methods. Our results indicate a consistent increase in gross primary production (GPP) across Asia since 2000, as shown by most bottom-up estimates. However, notable regional discrepancies emerged, particularly in Southeast Asia, where process-based models exhibited interannual variability that differed substantially from remote sensing–based and data-driven estimates. For net land–atmosphere CO₂ fluxes, represented by net biome production (NBP), substantial inconsistencies were observed among bottom-up estimates. While process-based models generally suggested a weak trend toward enhanced carbon sink strength, remote sensing–based and data-driven approaches indicated a more pronounced increase in net carbon uptake. These discrepancies highlight the need to better understand the underlying causes of divergence among bottom-up estimation approaches. Improved integration of satellite observations and bottom-up modeling frameworks will be essential to enhance the accuracy and reliability of terrestrial carbon budget assessments across Asia.

Fusing Geostationary and Polar-orbiting Satellite Data for Hourly, 100m All-weather Surface Temperature Modeling
presentations.abstract: High spatiotemporal resolution land surface temperature (LST) data is essential for monitoring ecosystem dynamics, yet current satellite sensors enforce a tradeoff between spatial detail and temporal frequency. Additionally, cloud cover creates significant data gaps in thermal infrared observations. To address these challenges, we present a unified framework generating hourly, 100-m, all-weather LSTs by coupling geostationary (GOES-R) and polar-orbiting satellite data. Our approach integrates two novel models. First, we address cloud obstruction using ‘C-SWARM’, a physics-based Surface Energy Balance model. Theoretically, C-SWARM treats daytime LST as a cloud-moderated warming process, explicitly modeling the competition between solar heating and atmospheric insulation. Validation at 49 flux tower sites demonstrates accuracy improvements of 0.38–1.89 K over benchmark gap-filling methods. Second, ‘UnmixGO’ employs stepwise temperature unmixing to downscale hourly GOES-R LST images from 2 km to 100 m. By utilizing spatially adaptive endmembers to constrain the solution space, UnmixGO avoids error amplification, outperforming conventional downscaling methods by 1.11 K in validation against real imagery. This framework effectively bridges the scale gap and overcomes weather limitations, providing a generalized solution for monitoring surface energy exchanges at local scales across hemispheric domains.

presentations.presentation_title: Super-resolution Sentinel-2 Imagery to Planetscope Using CNN: Application for River Morphology Classification
presentations.abstract: Enhancing River Morphology Mapping via Sentinel-2 Super-Resolution.While Super-Resolution (SR) is often used to bridge the spatial gap between free Sentinel-2 (10 m) imagery and commercial PlanetScope (~3 m) data, its effectiveness is frequently judged by image fidelity rather than its utility in environmental mapping. This study introduces a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) framework designed to enhance Sentinel-2 reflectance to a 3 m effective resolution, using PlanetScope imagery as the supervisory target. Beyond standard metrics like PSNR and SSIM, the SR performance was evaluated based on its ability to reconstruct critical riverine structures, such as channel edges and narrow riparian strips.To test the practical benefits, a Random Forest (RF) classifier was employed to map four distinct river corridor classes: water, sediment, trees, and grass. The study compared the classification performance of the original 10 m imagery against the 3 m SR product using identical training samples and validation designs. The results indicate that the CNN-based SR model produces sharper, more continuous features than traditional upsampling methods. Specifically, the SR-enhanced data significantly improved the separability of spectrally similar classes at sub-reach scales.Compared to the 10 m baseline, the SR workflow yielded higher macro-averaged F1-scores and more coherent spatial patterns for waterlines and sediment bars. This research demonstrates that SR provides tangible gains for downstream river morphology tasks, offering a cost-effective and transferable solution for high-frequency monitoring in data-sparse regions where commercial imagery may be inaccessible. presentations.presentation_title: Estimating Net Ecosystem Exchange in Climate-vulnerable Australian Tall Eucalypt Forests Using Geostationary Satellite Data
presentations.abstract: Tall eucalypt forests are unique to Australia and are most extensively distributed within Tasmania’s Wilderness World Heritage Area (TWWHA), where they form some of the most global carbon-dense forests and play an important role in regional and national carbon budgets due to their exceptionally high rates of carbon uptake. Recently, it was found that these forests exhibit an unusually high sensitivity to temperature, with forest carbon uptake declining sharply as temperatures rise, even when water and radiation are not limiting. Under continued climate warming, this heightened temperature sensitivity is expected to accelerate carbon loss and increase the risk of crossing irreversible carbon-balance tipping points. Although an eddy covariance flux tower (AU-Wrr) operated in the TWWHA from 2013 provided half-hourly measurements of ecosystem carbon flux, the tower has recently ceased operation, leaving carbon sequestration difficult to assess. In this study, we develop multiple machine learning models that integrate high-frequency Himawari geostationary satellite observations with climate data to estimate hourly net ecosystem exchange (NEE) at both site and regional scales. Model predictions are validated against eddy covariance measurements from AU-Wrr, demonstrating strong agreement with observed NEE (R² = 0.80; RMSE = 7.24 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹). Applying the trained model across the TWWHA reveals pronounced spatial variability in carbon exchange across diurnal and seasonal timescales. The northern regions act as a net carbon sink primarily between July and November, while during the rest of the year much of the TWWHA functions as a net carbon source. This study demonstrates the capability of geostationary satellite data to estimate hourly NEE and provides new insights into carbon sequestration dynamics in a globally significant forest ecosystem that is highly vulnerable to climate warming.

presentations.presentation_title: Spatio-temporal Deep Learning for Rapid and Robust Wildfire Detection Leveraging High-frequency Geostationary Scans
presentations.institution: Interdisciplinary Program in Earth Environmental System Science and Engineering, Kangwon National University, Chuncheon, South Korea
presentations.abstract: The increasing frequency and intensity of wildfires pose a severe threat to global carbon cycles, air quality, and ecosystem stability. Effective mitigation relies heavily on rapid ignition detection; however, current satellite-based monitoring systems often face a trade-off between temporal latency and detection accuracy. This study presents a novel framework for near real-time wildfire detection that leverages the high-frequency observation capabilities of the GEO-KOMPSAT-2A satellite, utilizing its unique 2-minute "Local Area" scan mode. To overcome the limitations of traditional static thresholding methods, which often struggle to differentiate between ignition points and solar artifacts, we employ a spatio-temporal deep learning approach. By treating satellite imagery as a dynamic sequence rather than isolated snapshots, the model analyzes the temporal evolution of heat signatures across visible, near-infrared, and thermal bands. This method effectively captures the distinct acceleration patterns of early-stage fires, filtering out transient noise such as glint. Our results demonstrate that this approach can identify ignitions in under 10 minutes, significantly faster than standard benchmarks, providing a critical window for intervention. This work highlights the potential of high-frequency geostationary data to support next-generation national early-warning systems, offering a scalable solution for minimizing the ecological and societal impacts of catastrophic wildfires.

presentations.presentation_title: Deciphering Spatiotemporal Heterogeneity of Carbon Fluxes on the Tibetan Plateau: a Daily, 500m NEE Dataset (2000–2024) via Mechanism-constrained Machine Learning
presentations.abstract: The Tibetan Plateau (TP) plays a pivotal role in the global carbon cycle given its complex terrain and high ecosystem heterogeneity. However, driven by scarce training sites and insufficient spatiotemporal resolution, existing products fail to capture daily-scale ecological transient processes and short-term external forcing events. To bridge this gap, we synthesized the most comprehensive dataset to date (~40 eddy covariance sites, including 16 newly processed stations and literature-shared data) and developed a novel mechanism-constrained machine learning framework to generate a high-spatiotemporal resolution (500 m, daily) Net Ecosystem Exchange (NEE) dataset for the TP spanning 2000–2024.By fusing satellite (MODIS) and reanalysis (ERA5-Land) data, we dissected NEE control mechanisms via the Atmosphere-Vegetation-Soil nexus. The framework incorporates three strategies: (1) PFT-based stratification to physically isolate conflicting ecological mechanisms; (2) Asymmetric feature engineering guided by Liebig's Law (e.g., decoupling moisture noise in energy-limited meadows vs. emphasizing root-zone soil moisture in water-limited deserts); and (3) Specialized logic for transition zones (ecotones) to handle mixed signals.Rigorous Leave-One-Site-Out (LOSO) validation shows that our mechanism-constrained model significantly outperforms traditional universal models and monthly-scale products, particularly in capturing the phenology of alpine meadows and pulse responses of steppes to short-term climate forcing. The resulting 25-year dataset unveils fine-scale spatiotemporal patterns of carbon source/sink strength over the TP. Specifically, we utilize this dataset to elucidate asynchronous responses of carbon sequestration capacity across alpine ecosystems to "warming and wetting" trends, track spatial variability of soil moisture stress, and identify "hidden" carbon sink hotspots previously masked by coarse-resolution products. This study demonstrates the potential of integrating high-spatial satellite observations with mechanism-informed AI to bridge the scale gap in ecosystem monitoring.

presentations.presentation_title: High-resolution Inverse Modelling of Greenhouse Gas Fluxes Over South Asia Using the Ground-based Monitoring and Gosat Satellite Observations.
presentations.abstract: We present a summary of using the ground-based monitoring and GOSAT satellite observations in the top-down estimates of country scale emissions and removals of carbon dioxide and methane made with a global high resolution global inverse model NTFVAR. GOSAT satellite retrievals are used with Obspack data and Indian regional data for 2010-2024 period. Long term regional carbon fluxes show a good balance globally with a modest tropical source. Comparison with observations over India suggests that reproducing the observed CO 2 seasonal cycle in the model and improving the carbon sink estimates can be achieved by adding surface observations over India to supplement a lack of satellite observations during the rainy season. Methane emissions estimates use EDGAR database for anthropogenic emissions combined with a set of natural flux categories. Country-scale analysis of the estimated methane anthropogenic emissions reveals that the top-emitting countries, including India, show differences with their respective inventories to be within the uncertainty range of the inventories, confirming that the posterior anthropogenic emissions did not deviate from nationally reported values. The model corrections to methane emissions for the major emitting countries were within the uncertainty range of inventories. The validity of the estimated methane fluxes for India is confirmed with aircraft observations of vertical profiles in troposphere. The key advantages of our approach were: (1) use of high-resolution transport, useful for simulations near anthropogenic emission hotspots, (2) prior anthropogenic emissions adjusted to the UNFCCC reports, (3) combining surface and satellite observations, which improves the estimation of both natural and anthropogenic fluxes over spatial scale of countries.

presentations.presentation_title: Seasonal Climate-driven Co2 Flux Variability in Northern Mid-to-high Latitudes
presentations.abstract: Not only CO 2 fluxes in the tropics, those across northern mid-to-high latitudes (30°N–90°N) also play a critical role in shaping year-to-year changes in the global carbon budget, yet its climatic drivers remain incompletely understood. We estimated non-fossil CO 2 fluxes using Greenhouse gases Observing SATellite (GOSAT) columnar CO 2 observations (XCO 2 ) as well as a state-of-the-art inversion method, and investigated the dominant drivers of CO 2 flux anomalies after establishing the absence of a detectable ENSO signals in this latitude band. Monthly and annual mean analyses reveal weak climate-flux relationships, motivating a seasonally stratified approach to explore. Two seasons were mainly examined: the growing season (May–September), when photosynthetic uptake is active and potentially water-limited, and the post-growing season (October–December), when respiration and phenological transitions dominate.Our analysis reflects strong phenological and hydrological modulation of biospheric processes at high latitudes. During the growing season, CO 2 flux anomalies exhibit significant and opposing relationships with temperature () and soil moisture (). Partial correlation analysis demonstrates that both the drivers exert statistically independent influences on flux variability, while standardized multiple regression indicates comparable contributions (), jointly explaining 47% of interannual variance. Composite analysis further shows that the extreme CO 2 emission years coincide with severe growing-season drought ( soil-moisture anomalies). In contrast, post-growing season flux variability is primarily temperature-driven, with weak and non-independent soil-moisture effects (). These results highlight growing-season drought as the primary driver of northern mid-to-high latitude CO 2 flux anomalies, with temperature acting as a seasonally dependent modulator.

presentations.presentation_title: Evaluation of Satellite Observation Data Bias for Use in Carbon Flux Analysis
presentations.abstract: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) launched the Global Greenhouse Gas Watch (G3W) in 2024 to estimate global greenhouse gas concentrations and fluxes, including CO₂, at 1° spatial and monthly temporal resolution, with one-month latency between concentration observations and flux estimations. Due to limitations in current observation networks, satellite data is essential to achieve this goal.Currently, multiple greenhouse gas monitoring satellites are operated by countries such as those in Europe, the U.S., and Japan, with more launches planned. To effectively use these datasets, it is vital to correct spatial and temporal biases unique to each satellite. Without correction, significant errors may affect flux estimates.In this study, we investigated the spatiotemporal variation of bias for greenhouse gas observation satellites (GOSAT, OCO-2, GOSAT-2) launched and operated in Japan and the United States using independent inversion analyses. GOSAT (2009–) has the longest observation period but exhibited a negative bias that varies seasonally, particularly over oceans. OCO-2 (2014–) has the widest observation coverage among the three satellites and also exhibited a relatively small bias. GOSAT-2 (2018–) has a wider observation coverage than GOSAT but showed a large overall positive bias.We successfully incorporated satellite observation data, corrected using independent inversion analysis, into the inverse analysis alongside in-situ observations. While bias correction successfully eliminated the influence of satellite observation data bias, the substantial increase in observation points resulted in changes in the analyzed global and regional-scale carbon dioxide fluxes. This was particularly evident in land areas where the proportion of satellite observation data was relatively large, compared to inverse analyses using in-situ observations alone. presentations.presentation_title: Long-term Greenhouse Gas Observations by GOSAT Series Satellites and NIES Products
presentations.abstract: The Greenhouse Gases Observing SATellite (GOSAT) and its successor, GOSAT-2, collectively known as the GOSAT series, have observed carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) and methane (CH 4 ) since 2009 and 2018, respectively, providing one of the longest and most consistent global greenhouse gas (GHG) observation records from space. Jointly developed by the National Institute for Environmental Studies (NIES), the Ministry of the Environment, Japan, and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), the series aims to advance scientific understanding of global CO 2 and CH 4 cycles and to support climate research and related policymaking.NIES is responsible for higher-level data processing, validation and distribution of GOSAT data products. Observational data are routinely processed at NIES data processing systems and distributed through the GOSAT data platforms. The product suite spans multiple processing levels: calibrated radiance spectra (Level 1); retrieved results of the global column-averaged dry-air mole fractions of CO 2 and CH 4 (XCO 2 and XCH 4 ; Level 2) etc.; gridded and temporally averaged concentrations (Level 3); and CO 2 and CH 4 surface flux estimates derived through inverse modeling (Level 4A), along with simulated concentrations (Level 4B). The Level 2 XCO 2 and XCH 4 products are validated with observations from the Total Carbon Column Observing Network (TCCON), a global ground-based network of solar-viewing Fourier transform spectrometers. These products have contributed essential datasets to major climate assessments, including the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report, and were submitted to the first Global Stocktake in 2022 under the Paris Agreement.The third satellite in the series, the Global Observing SATellite for Greenhouse gases and Water cycle (GOSAT-GW), launched in June 2025, carries the TANSO-3 grating spectrometer with wide and focus observation modes for monitoring XCO 2 , XCH 4 , and nitrogen dioxide from local to global scales. Product processing is ongoing, and the resulting datasets will support global GHG monitoring and verification of national anthropogenic emission inventories.

presentations.presentation_title: New Insights from The GOSAT-GW Greenhouse Gases Observation Mission for Climate Change Policy
presentations.abstract: The Japanese Global Observing SATellite for Greenhouse gases and Water cycle (GOSAT-GW) is an Earth-observing satellite to conduct global observations of atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO 2 ), methane (CH 4 ), and nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ) simultaneously from a single platform. GOSAT-GW is the third satellite in the series of the currently operating Greenhouse gases Observing SATellite (GOSAT) and GOSAT-2. One of its two sensors, the Total Anthropogenic and Natural emissions mapping SpectrOmeter-3 (TANSO-3) is a high-resolution grating spectrometer designed to measure the column-averaged dry-air mole fractions of CO 2 and CH 4 (denoted as XCO 2 and XCH 4 , respectively), as well as the vertical column density of tropospheric NO 2 , by utilizing the wavelength bands of 0.45, 0.76, and 1.61 µm for NO 2 , O 2 , and CO 2 and CH 4 , retrievals, respectively. GOSAT-GW flies in a sun-synchronous orbit with a local overpass time of approximately 13:30 and a 3-day ground-track repeat cycle. The TANSO-3 sensor has two observation modes in the push-broom operation: Wide Mode, which provides globally covered maps with a 10-km spatial resolution within 3 days, and Focus Mode, which provides snapshot maps over targeted areas with a high spatial resolution of 1–3 km. The objectives of the GOSAT-GW mission include (1) monitoring atmospheric global-mean concentrations of greenhouse gasses (GHGs), (2) verifying national anthropogenic GHG emissions inventories, and (3) detecting GHG emissions from large sources, such as megacities and power plants. With a projected operational lifetime of seven years, GOSAT-GW will provide vital space-based constraints on both anthropogenic and natural GHG emissions. The results of the first-light measurements will be presented, possibly in comparison to other satellites and the TCCON and COCCON observations.

presentations.presentation_title: Decoding the Spatio-temporal Dynamics within the Benthic Foraminiferal Community Structure from the Northeast Coastal Bay of Bengal
presentations.institution: Indian Institute of Science Education and Research Kolkata
presentations.abstract: Benthic foraminiferal assemblages are widely used as bioproxy for coastal environment monitoring. The present study investigated the seasonal variation within benthic foraminiferal assemblages and their co-occurrence patterns in response to freshwater influx and nutrient dynamics along the northeast coastal Bay of Bengal. Over a one-year period (2021–2022), benthic foraminiferal communities, sediment total organic carbon, and dissolved nutrient concentrations in surface and porewater were analyzed from intertidal zones spanning Junput and Tajpur. The benthic foraminiferal standing crop was high during the post-monsoon season (250 to 370 individuals) and declined in the pre-monsoon months (200 to 280 individuals). The benthic foraminiferal assemblages were dominated by Asterorotalia trispinosa, Ammonia sp.1, and Ammonia sp.2. Notably, Asterorotalia trispinosa showed a significant positive correlation with monsoonal rainfall and sediment total organic carbon, suggesting its potential as a reliable bioproxy for monsoon-influenced environments. Network analysis revealed the negative interactions between Asterorotalia trispinosa and members of Ammonia spp., while Asterorotalia trispinosa positively co-occurred with Trochammina inflata and Quinqueloculina seminula during the monsoon. Pearson correlation and Structural equation modeling revealed that surface and porewater concentrations of dissolved nitrate and ammonia, along with precipitation, were key environmental drivers affecting the spatio-temporal dynamics and interspecies interactions within the foraminiferal communities. These findings highlight the responses of benthic foraminifera to episodic nutrient enrichment and freshwater input and underscore their utility in ecological monitoring and paleoenvironmental reconstructions across tropical estuarine systems.

presentations.presentation_title: Recycling of Polyphosphate Under Phosphorus Limitation in the Pearl River Estuary
presentations.institution: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Studies on polyP dynamics have largely focused on oligotrophic systems, even though eutrophic ecosystems can also experience P deficiency due to excessive nitrogen inputs. In this study, we examined polyP dynamics in the eutrophic yet P-limited Pearl River Estuary region across the nutrient-rich estuarine waters to offshore regions along a nutrient gradient. We observed a similar "P deficiency response" compared to that in oligotrophic systems, indicating the accumulation of polyP under P limitation. Using combined analysis of various P species relative to biomass indicators, as well as meta-omic analyses, we found that polyP was actively recycled and remained relatively stable compared to other particulate P forms even under P deficiency. We observed that this recycling of polyP was linked to many functional cellular metabolic pathways. Taxonomy analysis further confirmed the close relationship between polyP dynamics and community compositions. Together, these findings further advance our understanding of the multifaceted functions of polyP in aquatic ecosystems under P-limiting conditions.

presentations.presentation_title: Integration of New Trace Gas Analyzers Into a Collection of Campbell Scientific Eddy Covariance Flux Systems Through Easyflux Upgrade
presentations.abstract: TGA300 series represent the new generation of legendary fast response Trace Gas Analyzer (e.g., TGA200A) for applications of CH 4 or N 2 O flux measurements in a wide spectrum of environments and conditions. Compared to its precursors, TGA300 widens its frequency response bandwidth, narrows its accuracy range, and has more auto controls for stable measurements while designed with minimized aerodynamic impacts for installations on a tripod or light tower in support of an eddy covariance flux system. Through the EasyFlux upgrade, it is compatible with any type of eddy covariance flux systems manufactured by Campbell Scientific (CS). Its integration with IRGASON (Integrated CO 2 ─H 2 O Open-Path Gas Analyzer and 3D Sonic Anemometer), CSAT3A (3D sonic anemometer) and EC150 (CO 2 ─H 2 O Open-Path Gas Analyzer), or CPEC306/310 (CO 2 ─H 2 O Close-Path Eddy-Covariance flux system) can measure the fluxes of CH 4 /N 2 O, CO 2 , H 2 O, sensible heat, and momentum. Its cost-efficient integration with CSAT3B/H only (3D sonic anemometer with a heating option) also can measure the fluxes of CH 4 /N 2 O and momentum if other flux values are not desired. The integration is enhanced through the applications of a CR6/CR1000Xe/Granite9 Datalogger and Volt116 Analogue Input Module to include all micrometeorological sensors which are commonly necessary along with field eddy-covariance flux systems. The integration and the enhancement are supported and realized by an update of the software package (EasyFlux). Here we present our efforts and progress on this subject in an attempt to advance the eddy covariance technology and provide more measurement options to the flux community.

presentations.presentation_title: An Estimate of Bacterial Bioelectricity in the Biosphere
presentations.abstract: Bacteria in the Biosphere conduct a substantial number of metabolic transactions per unit of time. This inquiry attempts to broadly estimate the number of electrons per unit volume per unit time within the Biosphere as a whole.The bacterial ecosystem is a significant contributor to the total biogeochemical process budget of Planet Earth affecting the biosphere’s environmental conditions and occupants across scales of space and time. By better understanding the bacterial bioelectrical system of the Biosphere, we may be able to better evaluate and consider the causes and effects of changes within the Biosphere over time and space. This inquiry utilizes information obtained from the scientific literature as referenced below. The sources are discussed within each component of the evaluation. The evaluations include the published estimates of the Biosphere dimensions, bacterial population, and metabolic rates. The information is utilized to calculate electron transfer rates per unit volume and an estimate of the range of bacterial electron transfer rates within the Biosphere. It is noted that the scarcity of available information limits the resolution of the outputs. The calculated electron transfer capacity is estimated to be in the range of 100 Faradays/km 3 /sec.

presentations.presentation_title: Long-term Changes in the Functional Species Composition of Japanese Forests Under a Changing Climate
presentations.abstract: Climate change affects establishment and survival of trees in the forests by modifying the boundaries of the environmental conditions suitable for them. This can lead to changes in forest composition, such as shifting to plant functional types (PFTs) favouring warmer and drier conditions. Shifting PFT compositions will influence biodiversity conservation, ecosystem services, and economic income, yet despite its importance, this process is still not fully examined. In this study, we analysed long-term forest monitoring data from plots stretching over Japan to investigate whether there is a detectable shift in PFT composition depending on latitude, age, forest type, and other factors. We found that evergreen broadleaf (EB) trees increased in abundance between the first and final years of the surveys at several locations, independent of forest type, age and latitude. Saplings of boreal conifer (BC) trees and deciduous broadleaf (DB) trees also largely increased in abundance, whereas older trees decreased in abundance, with mature BC trees showing the highest mortality. Temperate conifer (TC) trees displayed an opposite pattern, with saplings decreasing in abundance and older trees keeping stable numbers. The least and most diverse forests had stable levels of abundances, indicating high resilience to changes in PFT composition, although the species composition of saplings became more similar among forest plots compared to the composition of older trees. While the dominant PFT remained unaltered in most plots, traditionally DB and TC dominant forests were more sensitive to EB intrusion over the years. Sudden changes in some forest plots indicated that indirect effects of climate change, such as the increased frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, might have a greater impact than slower, sustained changes in temperature and precipitation. Our results can contribute to better management decisions in the conservation and forestry sectors to mitigate the negative impacts of climate change.

presentations.presentation_title: The Impacts of Oil Palm Expansion on Land Carbon Cycle in Southeast Asia
presentations.abstract: Rising demand for palm oil has driven rapid expansion of oil palm plantations in Southeast Asia over the past decades, yet their impacts on the regional carbon budget remain poorly constrained due to complex interactions between oil palm ecosystems and climate change, stand age, soils, and management. Here, we develop a diagnostic terrestrial biosphere model that incorporates key processes of oil palm carbon cycles, driven by high-resolution remote-sensing products and meteorological forcings. We validate our model using extensive observational data, including 31 site-years of carbon flux observations from eddy covariance sites and 360 sub-national yield records, and then simulate the carbon dynamics from 2001 to 2020 across Indonesia and Malaysia. Our model reproduces the observed carbon fluxes well, with R 2 > 0.90 and RMSE < 502 gC/m 2 /year against eddy covariance measurements. We find oil palm plantations initially (yrs < 10 years) act as strong carbon sources, with annual net ecosystem exchange (excluding harvested fruits) exceeding 2,000 gC/m 2 /year. The plantations approach carbon neutrality and can become net sinks on mineral soils after maturity (yrs > 10 years), whereas those on peat soils remain net sources in their lifetime. Our study reveals the controlling factors of oil palm carbon fluxes and provides a spatially explicit estimate of carbon fluxes across oil palm plantations, offering insight into their contribution to the regional carbon budget.
